Warum Merz beim Ukraine-Kredit aufs Ganze geht

Präsentiert von YouTube Von HANS VON DER BURCHARD Mit FERDINAND KNAPP PRÄSENTIERT VON Schicken Sie uns Ihre Tipps hier oder hier | X @vonderburchard @

Präsentiert von YouTube

Von HANS VON DER BURCHARD

Mit FERDINAND KNAPP

PRÄSENTIERT VON

Schicken Sie uns Ihre Tipps hier oder hier | X @vonderburchard @R_Buchsteiner | Das Playbook anhören oder online lesen

Moin Berlin, hier schreibt der mit Irish Stew und Guinness gestärkte Hans von der Burchard. Es ist Freitag, der 13.: Hoffentlich kein schlechtes Omen für den zweiten Gipfeltag in Dublin.

Dort droht ohnehin viel Streit: über den neuen Ukraine-Kredit, den Merz durch seine Haushalts-Drohung zum Chefthema beim Gipfel gemacht hat, und über die Frage, wer Europa in den künftigen Russland-Ukraine-Verhandlungen vertreten soll. Immerhin: Moskau ist offenbar bereit, Europa einen Platz am Verhandlungstisch zu gewähren. Auch dazu gleich mehr.

Derweil im Regierungsviertel: Die zur Abstimmung stehenden Geheimdienst-Reformen, die Ergebnisse aus der Bereinigungssitzung (es ging bis kurz sechs!) und Neues von der Linkspartei (dazu Co-Vorsitzender Luigi Pantisano im 200-Sekunden-Interview).

Reingehört: Im Samstags-Podcast nehmen sich Gordon Repinski und Rasmus Buchsteiner die innenpolitische Woche vor. Am Sonntag sortiert Claudia Major im Security Sunday die großen außenpolitischen Baustellen.

**(Anzeige) Eine Nachricht von YouTube: Verlässliche Partnerschaft seit über 15 Jahren: Seit 2007 teilt YouTube die Mehrheit seiner Werbeerlöse direkt mit Verlagen, Sendern und Medienschaffenden. Allein in den vier Jahren 2021-2024 flossen weltweit mehr als 100 Milliarden US-Dollar an Urheber*innen, Künstler*innen und Medienunternehmen. Das schafft Stabilität im digitalen Wandel. Hier mehr erfahren zum wirtschaftlichen Beitrag von YouTube.**

SEITE EINS

MERZ MACHT DRUCK: Unbeeindruckt davon, ob es andere „Erpressung“ nennen (der Slowake Robert Fico), „nicht unbedingt die richtige Richtung“ (Ungarns Péter Magyar) oder „keine besonders gute Diskussion“ (Tschechiens Andrej Babiš): Der Kanzler gibt nicht nach.

Kein EU-Haushalt ohne Ukraine-Unterstützung durch alle: Die deutsche Drohung wird beim zweiten EU-Gipfeltag in Dublin ein großer Konfliktpunkt. Doch Merz hat mehrere Gründe für seine Hartnäckigkeit.

Erstens: Trittbrettfahrerei und Sonderbehandlungen nicht mehr zulassen. Nach der Abwahl Viktor Orbáns, der die EU dauerhaft blockiert und lahmgelegt hatte, will Merz solche Tendenzen gleich im Keim ersticken. Zumal es bei der Unterstützung der Ukraine gegen Putins Angriffskrieg um eine essenzielle Frage der europäischen Sicherheit geht.

Zweitens: Mit der bevorstehenden Verabschiedung des EU-Haushalts, die nur alle sieben Jahre fällig ist, hat Deutschland als größter Beitragszahler ein seltenes Druckmittel zur Verfügung: Denn die Slowakei, Tschechien und Ungarn sind sehr stark von den Haushaltsgeldern der EU (und zum großen Teil eben aus Deutschland) abhängig.

Zu anderer Zeit kann ein Fico Nein sagen, ohne dass Merz viel dagegen tun kann (so geschehen letztes Jahr beim 90-Milliarden-Kredit für die Ukraine).

Diesmal ist es anders, und Merz will das nutzen, um hier grundsätzlich einen Riegel vorzuschieben.

Kanzler-Basta: Es kann nicht sein, dass Deutschland zweimal zahlt — als größter Beitragszahler beim Haushalt und zusätzlich mit erhöhtem Einsatz beim Ukraine-Darlehen, nur weil sich einige Länder nicht beteiligen wollen. Die Ukraine-Unterstützung sei eine „gemeinsame europäische Aufgabe“, so Merz.

Es ist auch eine vorbeugende Maßnahme: In fünf Monaten könnte Marine Le Pen zur französischen Präsidentin gewählt werden. Und wer weiß, wie die Wahlen in Italien, Polen, Spanien oder Griechenland ausgehen. Da lohnt es sich, vorher Grundsätzliches festzuzurren.

Nur: Ob es so schlau von Merz war, seine Drohung durch einen Brief an EU-Ratspräsident António Costa quasi öffentlich zu machen, darüber gehen die Meinungen auseinander.

Einige finden, Merz hätte das besser leise hinter verschlossenen Türen geregelt. Andere sagen: Es brauchte diesen Druck, um das Thema auf die Tagesordnung zu setzen.

Klar ist: Die Haushaltsverhandlungen werden nun deutlich toxischer. Falls Fico & Co. ihren Widerstand heute nicht aufgeben, wird der Streit schon in zwei Wochen beim nächsten, komplett auf die EU-Haushaltsgespräche konzentrierten Gipfel in Brüssel erneut Thema.

Eine Geldfrage: 70 Milliarden Euro soll der Ukraine-Kredit für 2027 umfassen, wovon die EU zwei Drittel (45 Milliarden) übernehmen soll. Eventuell können auch 10 Milliarden ungenutzter Mittel des EU-Verteidigungsprogrammes SAFE genutzt werden, was die Last verringern würde. Zugleich soll es im EU-Haushalt weitere, längerfristige Ukraine-Hilfen geben.

STREITPUNKT ZWEI: Die Dauerbrenner-Frage, ob sich Europa nicht auf einen einzelnen Chefverhandler mit Putin einigen sollte.

Giorgia Meloni hat das Thema auf die Tagesordnung gesetzt: Sie steht mit Blick auf ihre Wahlen im nächsten Jahr unter Druck, weil bisher allein die E3 (Deutschland, Frankreich, Großbritannien) Europa vertreten haben. In Abu Dhabi war Italien dann aber doch dabei.

Dies setzt wiederum Donald Tusk unter Druck: Wenn Italien kommen darf, sollte Polen als Vertreter Osteuropas auch. Und siehe an: Beim Debriefing mit Jared Kushner und Steve Witkoff gestern Abend (siehe diplomatische Depesche) war Polen mit dabei. Aus E3 mach E5 …

Kaja Kallas findet: Ich bin die EU-Außenbeauftragte, lasst es mich doch machen. Das sorgt bei den meisten Regierungschefs jedoch nur für ein müdes Lächeln.

Merz stellt klar: Die E3, oder auch E5, seien „ein bewährtes Format“, so der Kanzler. „Ich sehe überhaupt kein Problem darin, dass das so bleibt.“ Macron sieht das ebenso.

Playbook-Prognose: Außer viel Gerede tut sich heute wenig.

Stimme von außen: Trumps früherer Ukraine-Sondergesandter Kurt Volker hält den deutschen Bundeskanzler für geeignet — favorisiert aber Nato-Generalsekretär Mark Rutte, wie er Annett Meiritz mitteilte. Eine weitere Option: ein ehemaliger Regierungschef, „der für ganz Europa sprechen kann“.

DIPLOMATISCHE DEPESCHE

DEBRIEF AUS MOSKAU: Kushner und Witkoff haben auf dem Rückflug einen Boxenstopp in Dublin eingelegt und Wolodymyr Selenskyj und die E5 über ihr Gespräch mit Putin gebrieft.

Bereits in Moskau verkündete Witkoff: „Die Europäer werden bei der nächsten Sitzung dabei sein, was wir für eine sehr große Sache halten, denn es ist wichtig — sie sind unsere Partner, und es ist wichtig, dass sie einbezogen werden.“ Mehr hier.

Und am Abend in Irland sagte Kushner: „Wir können dieses Abkommen nicht abschließen, ohne dass die Europäer mit am Verhandlungstisch sitzen.“

ZENTRALBANK-GEFEILSCHE: Die Bundesregierung dementiert einen Bericht von Frankreichs Le Point, wonach sich Merz und Emmanuel Macron auf den Spanier Pablo Hernández de Cos als nächsten Präsidenten der Europäischen Zentralbank geeinigt haben sollen.

Fakt ist: Die beiden sprachen gestern am Rande des Dublin-Gipfels. Aber bevor man sich einigt, muss Merz die Wahl (Gegenkandidat ist der Niederländer Klaas Knot) ohnehin noch mit der SPD absprechen. Nothing is agreed until everything’s agreed …

Zeitplan: Bis zum EU-Gipfel in zwei Wochen (spätestens) soll die Einigung aber stehen.

Anzeige

HAUSHALT

GLEICH GEHT ES VOR DIE BLAUE WAND: Die Chefhaushälter der Fraktionen kommen ab 9 Uhr in die Bundespressekonferenz — erst ist die AfD dran, dann Grüne und Linke, um 11 Uhr schließlich Union und SPD.

Der Reihe nach: Um 5:54 Uhr war zu Ende bereinigt im Haushalt. Alle Zahlen, Daten, Fakten der langen Haushaltsnacht hier. Rasmus Buchsteiner, Jasper Bennink und Louis Westendarp waren vor Ort im Paul-Löbe-Haus.

Unterm Strich: Die Neuverschuldung im Kernhaushalt steigt gegenüber dem Regierungsentwurf aus dem Sommer um 4,2 Milliarden Euro auf 118,727 Milliarden Euro. Die Sondervermögen für Bundeswehr und Infrastruktur mitgerechnet plant der Bund für 2027 mit neuen Krediten in Höhe von 210,41 Milliarden Euro.

Klar: Alles, was die Koalition in den letzten Tagen beschäftigt hat, ist natürlich nicht bereinigt: die Sache mit der Stromsteuer zum Beispiel. Oder die mit der kalten Progression.

Die CDU schiebt den Sozialdemokraten den Schwarzen Peter zu: „Ich bin ehrlicherweise etwas irritiert, was aus der SPD geworden ist. Sie war doch immer die Partei, die sich eingesetzt hat für die Menschen, die hart arbeiten, und plötzlich ist das … nicht so wichtig“, sagte Paul Ziemiak gestern in den Tagesthemen.

Anderes großes Sorgenthema: Die Bundesagentur für Arbeit und deren prekäre Finanzlage. Sie bekam in der Nacht drei zusätzliche Kreditmilliarden genehmigt.

Schlechte Nachrichten aus Nürnberg: Bis Ende 2027 wird das Defizit der Bundesagentur um 8,2 Milliarden auf 18,6 Milliarden Euro steigen. So jedenfalls die Prognose, die heute den Verwaltungsrat der Behörde beschäftigt.

Was diesmal war wie immer: Auch in dieser Bereinigungssitzung kamen viele Deckblätter viel später als versprochen. Und es gab jede Menge wartende Minister in Ledersesseln zu sehen.

Premiere: Natürlich hatte man den Kabinettsneulingen vorher gesagt, sie sollten besser frühzeitig da sein. Um 0:06 Uhr war Alexander Schweitzers Auftritt auch schon zu Ende. Steffen Bilger war der Nächste, während Carsten Linnemann sich auch schon bereit machte.

Interessant: Kurz bevor es im Ausschuss um den Verkehrsetat ging, bekam Cedric Looks dieses Blatt von den Haushältern: Der Bund verpflichtet sich zu vier zusätzlichen Milliarden für Bahnbauprojekte und möchte das durch Umschichtung aus dem Verteidigungsetat finanzieren. Alle Änderungen im Verkehrsbereich? Hier.

Kurz nach 5:00 Uhr: Boris Pistorius hat sich gerade als letzter Minister verabschiedet. Die Bereinigungssitzung geht in die Schlusskurve. Um 5:55 Uhr waren dann alle Zahlen da.

Der Blick geht jetzt nach vorn. Bis zum Koalitionsausschuss am Dienstag müsste eine Entlastungslösung her — Stichwort Stromsteuer und/oder kalte Progression. Die Nervosität in der Union ist so groß wie lange nicht.

Übrigens: Petra Köpping soll den Platz von Bärbel Bas im Koalitionsausschuss einnehmen.

AUSSER STIFTUNG NICHTS GEWESEN: Über den Entwicklungshaushalt wurde viel diskutiert, in einem Punkt sind sich aber alle einig: Die politischen Stiftungen sollen genug Geld bekommen.

Deshalb werden die geplanten Kürzungen um mehr als 100 Millionen Euro zurückgenommen — was eigentlich gegen die Prioritäten von Reem Alabali Radovan spricht.

Denn: Das BMZ will wirksamer werden. Doch ob die Vorhaben der Stiftungen tatsächlich wirken, wird nicht systematisch überprüft, hört Carlotta. Der Bundesrechnungshof hat zudem wiederholt Mängel bei Verwaltungskosten, Mittelverwendung und Steuerung festgestellt — zuletzt bei der KAS und der FES.

Immerhin: Das Geld für die Stiftungen kommt nicht aus dem Einzelplan 23, sondern aus dem Finanzministerium.

Die Verlierer sitzen woanders: Bei Hungerbekämpfung und Krisenvorsorge wird kräftig gekürzt — obwohl die Wirkung dieser Programme vielfach belegt ist. Die Mittel für die strukturbildende Übergangshilfe (KWI) sinken von 711 auf 435 Millionen Euro (minus 39 Prozent). Für Agrar- und Ernährungssysteme gibt es ein Drittel weniger.

PLENARSAALEBENE

DIENSTE NEU GEDACHT: Um 9 Uhr steht die Novellierung der Nachrichtendienste auf der Tagesordnung. Es ist die größte Reform von BND und Verfassungsschutz seit Jahren. Sie sollen im Zeitalter von Cyberangriffen, Sabotage und hybrider Kriegsführung deutlich offensiver agieren können.

Dickes Brett: Mehr als 80 Verhandlungsstunden sind in das Gesetz geflossen. „Das war das größte und intensivste Stück Arbeit, das mir je begegnet ist“, sagt einer der Verhandler zu Rixa Fürsen. Die wichtigsten Neuerungen:

— Aktive Cyberabwehr: Die Dienste sollen künftig nicht mehr nur beobachten, sondern auch Hacker-Infrastruktur ausschalten, technische Anlagen stören oder Waffen und Sprengmittel unbrauchbar machen.

— Wohnungen heimlich betreten: Der Verfassungsschutz und der BND sollen unter strengen Voraussetzungen Wohnungen ohne Wissen der Bewohner betreten dürfen, etwa zur Abwehr von Terror- oder Spionagegefahren.

— Mehr digitale Überwachung: Neue Befugnisse für IT-Zugriffe, KI-Auswertung und biometrische Gesichtserkennung.

— Längere Datenspeicherung: Der BND soll Kommunikationsinhalte bis zu sechs Monate und Verbindungsdaten bis zu 13 Monate speichern dürfen.

— Minderjährige als V-Leute: Künftig sollen unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen auch Jugendliche ab 16 Jahren als Vertrauenspersonen eingesetzt werden können.

— Mehr Fokus auf organisierte Kriminalität: Der Verfassungsschutz soll gegen kriminelle Netzwerke vorgehen dürfen, wenn diese verfassungsfeindliche Strukturen unterstützen.

— Neues Kontrollsystem: Der Unabhängige Kontrollrat erhält deutlich mehr Kompetenzen und soll Überwachungs- und Eingriffsmaßnahmen vorab genehmigen und überwachen.

Doch die neuen Befugnisse sorgen für Streit: Kritiker sehen die Trennung zwischen Polizei und Nachrichtendiensten gefährdet, Befürworter sprechen von einer überfälligen Anpassung an die Realität hybrider Bedrohungen.

Karlsruhe ruft: Über Teile der Reform wird am Ende das Bundesverfassungsgericht entscheiden müssen. Mehr dazu hat Welt-Kollege Lennart Pfahler hier aufgeschrieben.

PARTEIEN

MACHTKAMPF ÜBERSCHATTET VORSTANDSSITZUNG: Heute trifft sich der geschäftsführende Parteivorstand der Linken, am Samstag der erweiterte Parteivorstand, erfuhr Cedric Looks. Dabei sollte es eigentlich um Themen wie eine linke Bundespräsidentschaftskandidatin gehen…

…doch: Vanessa Emdes Fraktionsausschluss und die daraus resultierende parteiinterne Debatte um „Palästina-Solidarität“ überschatten auch diese Sitzung. Es wird an einer Erklärung gearbeitet, hört Cedric.

Denn im eigenen Parteivorstand sind Emde-Unterstützer, denen eine Klarstellung wichtig ist: Emdes Ausschluss dürfe nicht wegen ihrer „Palästina-Solidarität“, sondern höchstens wegen ihrer Provokationen (hier oder hier) passieren.

Auch eine Gruppe von Bundestagsabgeordneten arbeitet weiter an einer Palästina-Erklärung. Viel Zündstoff also für die Parteispitzen Ines Schwerdtner und Luigi Pantisano.

Pantisano sagt im 200-Sekunden-Interview, bei der Emde-Causa gehe es „nicht um die Frage, ob sie gegen das Existenzrecht Israels ist“, sondern um eine Lösung, in der jüdische Menschen und Palästinenser gemeinsam in einem Staat leben könnten. „Und das ist eine berechtigte Frage“, so der Co-Parteichef.

FRAKTIONSEBENE

PARTEICHEFIN MÖCHTE ABTRETEN, zumindest aus dem Haushaltsausschuss: Nach diesem Aufruf von unserem Machtwechsel-Kollegen Robin Alexander hat Cedric sich umgehört und kann bestätigen: Ines Schwerdtner möchte ihren Posten im mächtigsten Ausschuss im Parlament abgeben.

Die eigene Fraktion will den Wechsel: So war Schwerdtners seltene Anwesenheit immer wieder im Ausschuss Thema. Ihre Haushaltskollegen Dietmar Bartsch, Tamara Mazzi, Sascha Wagner und die Haushalts-Stellvertreter der Linken mussten Schwerdtner die Einzelpläne abnehmen.

Was denn nun? Auf Instagram sagte Schwerdtner, sie sei sowieso nur noch für das Sondervermögen zuständig. Cedric hört, dass sie offiziell aber eigentlich für noch mehr Einzelpläne zuständig sei.

Wie geht’s weiter? Chef-Haushälter Dietmar Bartsch sucht nun einen Nachfolger. Zum Jahresende soll es eine Entscheidung geben.

Wird es schon mal nicht: Nach seinem Rückzug aus dem Innenausschuss sucht Ferat Koçak eigentlich weiter einen neuen Ausschuss, in Bartschs Team wird er aber sicher nicht kommen. Aktuell ist er nur Stellvertreter im Kulturausschuss.

LÄNDERPUNKTE

SCHLINGERKURS: In der vergangenen Woche haben die Parlamentarier im Eiltempo die Führerscheinreform durchgebracht, doch nun hakt es auf den letzten Metern: Die Verordnung, in der die Reduzierung von Theorieunterricht, Sonderfahrten oder der Prüfungszeit geregelt wird, kann nicht (wie geplant) im November verabschiedet werden.

Daran liegt es: Es gibt insbesondere beim Thema Verkehrssicherheit noch Bedenken. Hier meldet das Saarland Beratungsbedarf, dessen Verkehrsministerin Petra Berg auch Sprecherin für alle SPD-Länder ist, wie Cedric erfahren hat.

Zeitplan: Die für die Preissenkungen zentrale Verordnung soll nun erst im Dezember vom Bundesrat beschlossen werden, das zugehörige Gesetz der Bundestagsabgeordneten soll aber wie geplant nächste Woche von der Länderkammer verabschiedet werden.

BAND DES BUNDES

LEERE REGIERUNGSFLIEGER: Obwohl Berlin seit 1999 Regierungssitz und der BER seit 2020 in Betrieb ist, sind die Regierungsflugzeuge der Bundeswehr noch immer in Köln-Wahn stationiert. Der Umzug ist für frühestens 2036 geplant, wie die Bundesanstalt für Immobilienaufgaben dem Spiegel mitteilte.

Allein 798 Bereitstellungsflüge (Leerflüge von Köln nach Berlin und zurück) gab es 2025, wie eine Antwort der Bundesregierung auf eine kleine Anfrage der AfD-Fraktion vom Februar ergab.

EUROVISION

MACRON WILL WENGER ALS FIFA-CHEF: Frankreichs Präsident hat der Trainer-Legende Arsène Wenger Unterstützung für eine Kandidatur als FIFA-Präsident angeboten, wie unsere Kollegen vom Telegraph erfahren haben. Damit könnte Wenger gegen den von Trump unterstützten Gianni Infantino kandidieren.

TRANSATLANTIK

DER EINE WIRD ZURÜCKGEPFIFFEN: JD Vance soll sich künftig nicht mehr in die Kriegsdiplomatie mit dem Iran einbringen. Donald Trump erklärte gestern auf Truth Social, seinen Vize „angewiesen“ zu haben, sich auf die „massive Korruption und Kriminalität“ im Land zu konzentrieren.

„Wir brauchen keinen Deal mit dem Iran“, erklärte Trump. „Diese Tage sind lange vorbei. Wir haben ihr Geld. Wir haben ihre Meerenge.“

Auslöser? Am Mittwoch berichtete das Wall Street Journal, dass Vance ein persönliches Treffen mit dem iranischen Hardliner Mohsen Rezai vorbereite, um neue Wege zu einem Frieden zu sondieren.

DER ANDERE WACKELT: Im Weißen Haus wird in diesen Tagen aber vor allem über die Zukunft von US-Handelsminister Howard Lutnick beraten. Der wurde gestern gemeinsam mit dem nun zurückgetretenen Nvidia-Chef Jensen Huang vor den Kongress zitiert. Anfang Dezember sollen sie im Senat aussagen.

Not happy: Amtierende und ehemalige Regierungsvertreter werfen Lutnick vor, Nvidia zu wenig kontrolliert und Exportkontrollen nicht konsequent durchgesetzt und gegen Schmuggel gesichert zu haben — mehr dazu heute bei unseren Kollegen von DC Decoded.

**Gesponserte Umfrage: Wir möchten Ihre Meinung hören: Bitte nehmen Sie an einer einminütigen Umfrage zu einem unserer Werbepartner teil.**

SPOTTED

REMMO INTERNATIONAL: Die Berliner Clan-Größe Issa Remmo hat gestern an einem Symposium zu Islamismus im Europaparlament in Brüssel teilgenommen – kein Scherz. Eingeladen hatte die französische Getreidebäuerin und Abgeordnete Céline Imart aus der EVP-Fraktion, der auch die CDU angehört.

WIE HEISST DER KLEINE DENN: Bei den vielen namentlichen Abstimmungen im Bundestag gestern kamen viele Abgeordnete mit Babys in die Westlobby. Darunter: Jens Spahn mit Baby Georg. Nina Warken, Gitta Connemann, Lars Klingbeil, Julia Klöckner und Alexander Dobrindt begrüßten den Säugling verzückt.

AGENDA

— Die Regierungspressekonferenz findet um 12:15 Uhr statt.

— Weltklimakonferenz: In Antalya läuft die COP31 noch bis zum 20. November.

— Von der Pflege aufs Baufeld: Um 8:30 Uhr ist Karin Prien beim zweiten Tag des Deutschen Pflegetages in Berlin, um 16 Uhr greift sie in Lübeck zum Spaten für den Neubau des Trave-Campus der Handwerkskammer.

— Zurück auf der Schulbank: Um 9:50 Uhr besucht Alexander Schweitzer einen Berufssprachkurs in der Charité, setzt sich selbst in den Unterricht und spricht anschließend mit den Teilnehmern, bevor er ein Pressestatement gibt.

— Filmabend in Erfurt: Um 19 Uhr schaut sich Carsten Schneider den Film „Das kahle Herz – Waldmenschen in Thüringen“ an und diskutiert danach auf dem Podium.

— Feierabend beim Bauerntag: Um 20 Uhr hält Alois Rainer einen Vortrag beim Kreisbauerntag Weilheim-Schongau im oberbayerischen Eberfing.

Samstag:

— Silberjubiläum in Kreuzberg: Um 19 Uhr hält Frank-Walter Steinmeier eine Ansprache zum 25-jährigen Bestehen des Jüdischen Museums Berlin.

Um 12:30 Uhr legen Frank-Walter Steinmeier, der österreichische Bundespräsident Alexander Van der Bellen, Julia Klöckner und Pistorius gemeinsam mit den Spitzen von Bundesrat, Verfassungsgericht, Berliner Senat und Bundeswehr Kränze an der Neuen Wache nieder. Um 13:30 Uhr folgt die zentrale Gedenkstunde des Volksbunds im Bundestag, bei der Van der Bellen die Gedenkrede hält und Steinmeier das Totengedenken spricht.

-Mercedes: Deutschland, nein danke

-Nividia: Der Skandal-Abgang des Gründers

-Steuern: Jetzt CDU gegen CSU

https://click.redaktion.handelsblatt.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTksInQiOjk5NzEsInMiOjd9AAcAAAAACU29TL9Jkwn5wGt7ayKPpuTGqWofzn7BPodB19SYPIG8ZJ4O2sVdXiq2b0I_K6F3G2_bDv1ErswxpGPxjB7PgHvNLXlvqRsXeo0FRDQ

Mercedes-Stern: Bye, bye Deutschland. (Foto: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa)

Guten Morgen, liebe Leserin, lieber Leser,kein Unternehmen steht so für Autobau in Deutschland wie Mercedes, schließlich wurde das Auto hier einst erfunden. Insofern hat die gestrige Nachricht nicht nur große Tragweite, sondern auch historische Ironie: Mercedes stoppt alle Investitionen in Deutschland.

Arbeitsdirektorin Britta Seeger schrieb im Intranet des Konzerns, wo mein Kollege Michael Scheppe auch gerne mal vobeischaut:

Kommen wir nicht zu einer Einigung, werden wir sehr harte Schritte gehen.

Gemeint sind neben dem Investitionsstopp auch die Schließung ganzer Werke in Deutschland und umfassende Verlagerungen ins Ausland. Es ist nicht ganz von der Hand zu weisen, dass man dieses Ansinnen in unschonen Worten als Erpressung beschreiben konnte. Allerdings eine okonomisch begründete: Eine Mischung aus Managementfehlern von CEO Ola Kallenius, einer daraus resultierenden Verkaufsschwache, die US-Zolle und das wegbrechende China-Geschaft setzen Mercedes unter Druck.

Im Kern will der Konzern, dass die Beschaftigten bei gleichem Lohn mindestens 38 statt wie bisher 35 Stunden (auf einer Vollzeitstelle) pro Woche arbeiten. Auch Weihnachts- und Urlaubsgeld sowie die Gewinnbeteiligung stehen zur Disposition, 800 Millionen Euro will der Vorstand so jahrlich sparen.

Der Grund ist leicht nachzuvollziehen: Im US-Werk Tuscaloosa sind die Arbeitskosten 17,9 Prozent niedriger als in deutschen Werken, im ungarischen Kecskemet, seit dem Sommer das großte Mercedes-Werk Europas, sogar 75 Prozent. Zugleich werden dort 33,1 beziehungsweise 27,5 Prozent mehr gearbeitet.

Die IG Metall dagegen halt an der 35-Stunden-Woche fest. Beide Seiten haben sich also eingegraben – nicht sehr zukunftstrachtig in einer Branche, die davon lebt, dass sich etwas bewegt.

Ex-Nvidia-Chef Jensen Huang: Viele Fragen sind noch offen. (Foto: Soeren Staceh/dpa)

Nvidia: Fall eines Ausnahmemanagers

Vom Chef des weltgroßten Konzerns zum Angeklagten in einer Staatsaffare vor dem US-Kongress, der ihn noch vor dem 26. November anhoren will: Jensen Huang, bis gestern 15 Uhr europaischer Zeit Chef des großten Chipherstellers der Welt, hat bewegte Wochen hinter sich. Das konnte als schillerndes Schicksal eines Managers, der über womoglich drei Affaren zu zwei Nividia-Managerinnen und einer mutmaßlichen China-Spionin stolperte, in Erinnerung bleiben. Wenn an der Personalie Huang nicht so viel mehr hinge.

Die großen Fragen dieser Affare sind noch offen: Bleibt Nvidia Taktgeber der KI-Revolution? Welche Rolle spielt künftig Huang in dem Konzern, an dem er weiter 3,6 Prozent der Aktien halt? Und ist über seine Affare Wissen nach China abgeflossen?

Was dagegen klar ist: Das Unternehmen leidet. Binnen einer Woche verlor Nvidia rund eine halbe Billion Dollar Borsenwert, gestern ging es da mit 4,3 Prozent schon fast glimpflich abwarts. Offen ist, wie es an der Spitze weitergeht. Interimschefin Colette Kress soll nur eine Ubergangslosung sein. US-Prasident Donald Trump schlug gestern Ex-Apple-Chef Tim Cook vor:

A Legend replaces a Legend!

Elon Musk wiederum nannte es „eine Ehre“, wenn er Huang bei SpaceX einstellen konnte. Das System der Tech-Bros mag aufgewirbelt sein – zu Ende ist es nicht. Notfalls stellen sich die Legenden eben gegenseitig ein.

CDU-Abgeordnete Christina Stumpp (Foto: Katharina Kausche/dpa)

Steuern: Jetzt CDU gegen CSU

Dass ihr Kanzler nicht verhandeln kann, beklagen CDU-Abgeordnete schon seit Beginn der schwarz-roten Koalition. Zu oft schien die SPD glücklicher aus Koalitionsgesprachen zu kommen als die Union. So vernehmbar wie nach der Haushaltseinigung am Mittwochabend war der Unmut aber noch nie. Vor allem, dass die CDU weder den Ausgleich der kalten Progression noch die Senkung der Stromsteuer durchsetzte, sorgt in der Fraktion für Frust. Die, allerdings gerade auch von Merz geschasste, Ex-Vize-Generalsekretarin Christina Stumpp soll in der Sitzung gesagt haben:

Dafür habe ich keinen Wahlkampf gemacht.

Der Frust ist so groß, dass die CDU nicht mehr nur gegen die SPD austeilt, sondern auch gegen die CSU. CDU-Haushaltspolitiker Mathias Middelberg sagte gestern RTL/ntv, Stromsteuersenkung oder Ausgleich der kalten Progression seien derzeit wichtiger als der Einstieg in die ausgeweitete Mütterrente – ein Lieblingsprojekt von CSU-Chef Markus Soder. CSU-Landesgruppenchef Alexander Hoffmann halt von solchen Ideen: nichts. Am Dienstag tagt der Koalitionsausschuss. Dort sitzen allerdings wieder die gleichen Verhandler wie bisher – denen sie in der eigenen Fraktion das Konnen absprechen.

EZB: Ein Deutscher als Chefvolkswirt?

Markus Brunnermeier ist einer der interessantesten deutschen Okonomen. Nicht nur, weil er in Princeton lehrt, sondern weil er zu jener neueren Generation deutscher Wirtschaftswissenschaftler gehort, die frei von Dogmen sind. Insofern ist es eine gute Nachricht, dass er Chefvolkswirt der Europaischen Zentralbank werden konnte.

Die Personalie soll Teil eines Pakets sein, auf das sich Kanzler Friedrich Merz und Frankreichs Prasident Emmanuel Macron bald einigen konnten. Frankreich würde auf den machtigen Chefvolkswirt-Posten verzichten, wenn im Gegenzug der Spanier Pablo Hernández de Cos auf Christine Lagarde folgt, die im Februar vorzeitig geht. Das Markte-Ressort, das im Ernstfall Staatsanleihen kauft, bekame die franzosische Ex-Ministerin Laurence Boone. Ein deutscher Professor soll also streng bleiben, wahrend eine Franzosin franzosische Anleihen kauft – in Notenbankkreisen fragt man sich, ob der Kanzler das zu Ende gedacht hat.

Rente: Mit der Aktie ins Alter

Selten waren sich Verbraucherschützer, Finanzbranche und Politik so einig: Das Altersvorsorgedepot, das ab dem 1. Januar die Riester-Rente ablost, gilt als „großer Wurf“. Die Forderung ist tatsachlich simpel. Auf die ersten 360 Euro Eigenbeitrag legt der Staat 50 Cent je Euro drauf, bis 1800 Euro sind es noch 25 Cent. Das macht maximal 540 Euro pro Person, dazu bis zu 300 Euro je Kind. Und anders als bei Riester muss nichts mehr garantiert werden – der Weg in die Aktie ist frei.

Entsprechend laut wirbt die Branche. Die Ratingagentur Scope rechnet mittelfristig mit 30 bis 50 Milliarden Euro Zufluss pro Jahr. Kein Wunder, dass der Finanzpsychologe Valentin Haas im Gesprach mit unserem Geldanlage-Chefreporter Markus Hinterberger bereits eine „Vorsorge-Fomo“ diagnostiziert. Ich finde ja, das klingt nicht schlecht – ich litt bisher eher unter Vorsorge-Prokrastination. Egal, welches Leiden Sie in Rentenfragen plagt: Die zwolf Antworten meines Kollegen zum Altersvorsorgedepot sollten lindernd wirken.

Die Verbraucher blicken wieder positiver auf die kommenden Wochen. Gerade die leichte Abnahme der Konsumzurückhaltung ist ein guter Startpunkt für das anstehende Weihnachtsgeschaft. Trotz optimistischerer Konjunkturerwartungen sind die Verbraucher allerdings weiterhin auf Sicherheit und finanzielle Vorsorge bedacht. In den nachsten Monaten wird sich damit der private Konsum noch nicht so kraftig erholen, dass er ein starker Treiber des gesamtwirtschaftlichen Wachstums ist.

Five Chinese Experts on How China and the US Should Talk About AI

Ahead of the next China-US AI talks, we asked leading experts what success looks like and how to build a lasting diplomatic channel.

Erik Lindblad and Kwan Yee Ng

Nov 12

READ IN APP

The story so far: In September, China and the United States agreed to launch an AI Dialogue to exchange views on risks and benefits related to AI, and the next round of talks was set for November. They also agreed to set up a bilateral communication channel for AI incidents.

According to media reports, AI cooperation is a potential deliverable to be announced when presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen next week.

Subscribed

The view from China: We asked five Chinese experts what they expect from the next China-US AI dialogue, what success would look like, and what they think Washington needs to understand about Beijing’s approach to international AI governance.

The five experts featured in this post are:

XIAO Qian (肖茜) – Vice Dean of the Institute for AI International Governance and Deputy Director of the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University

LU Chuanying (鲁传颖) – Professor and Vice Dean at the School of Political Science and International Relations, Tongji University

ZHANG Ling (张伶) – Senior Colonel (Ret.), Former Associate Professor of National Defense University

JIANG Tianjiao (江天骄) – Associate Professor, Development Institute, Fudan University

YAO Xu (姚旭) – Secretary-General of the Center for Global AI Innovative Governance and Associate Professor at the Development Institute, Fudan University

Key takeaways:

A realistic goal of the upcoming talks is a regular, predictable channel rather than expecting substantive outcomes at this early stage. Any incident reporting mechanism would need professional teams, robust procedures, and careful handling of information.

Experts see common ground on safety risks. Some argue that China’s own framing of cyber, bio, and loss-of-control risks closely mirrors US concerns, and that countering terrorist and criminal misuse of AI offers a natural entry point for cooperation.

To succeed, the dialogue requires political will and candid exchange.

Experts stress that China regards safety and development as mutually reinforcing, but expects to participate in global rule-setting on equal terms.

The bilateral dialogue can complement multilateral initiatives such as the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the World AI Cooperation Organization.

XIAO Qian (肖茜) is the Vice Dean of the Institute for AI International Governance and Deputy Director of the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University. She previously spent over a decade working at China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and at the Chinese Embassies in Russia and the United Kingdom.

What is your expectation for the upcoming AI talks between the US and China?

My expectation for the next AI talks is that the two sides should prioritize addressing issues of common concern, including the misuse of AI, and exchanging views on both the benefits and risks associated with AI. There have been some changes in the U.S. domestic political landscape following the midterm elections. The most realistic outcome would be to build on the consensus already reached and take a further step forward, such as the design of an incident-reporting mechanism, the types of incidents to be reported and the thresholds for reporting. Establishing standing working groups on both sides would help institutionalize the bilateral communication mechanism and make it more sustainable.

LU Chuanying (鲁传颖) is Professor and Vice Dean of the School of Political Science and International Relations at Tongji University. He is also Director of the Center for AI Political Science Research.

What is your expectation for the upcoming AI talks between the US and China?

That China and the United States can place institution building at the top of the agenda. This means being able to conduct regular exchanges and dialogues on key AI issues, insulated from external disruptions. At the same time, both sides can pursue concrete, pragmatic cooperation in specific areas, thereby gradually building mutual trust.

What are the most important next steps for the two sides to operationalize the bilateral incident reporting mechanism?

Drawing on experience from cybersecurity and other domains, incident reporting should be handled by professional teams and robust procedures. In addition, both sides should ensure strict confidentiality regarding the information shared by the other party.

What is the single most important factor to ensure the dialogue is a success? What is the single biggest risk for the bilateral dialogue?

Support from the leaders on both sides is critical to the success of the dialogue. In the current climate of bilateral relations, advancing cooperation faces too many uncertainties. Direct support from the leaders is the only factor capable of countering external pressures and disruptions. The single biggest risk is a prolonged failure to deliver tangible outcomes, which would lead outside observers to question both sides’ willingness and ability to cooperate.

ZHANG Ling (张伶) is a retired Senior Colonel (Army), who is a recipient of two Third-Class Merit Citations and a “Peace Mission” Medal. She holds degrees in computer science, cybersecurity, and national security strategy. Her research covers great power competition and international security, emerging technologies and the evolution of warfare, global digital security and governance, and digital literacy education.

What is your expectation for the upcoming AI talks between the US and China?

My expectation is for the dialogue to become a predictable, regularly convened mechanism where both sides can clearly articulate their respective concerns regarding AI risks. The single most critical factor for success is candor and the political will to cooperate. Any information or actions that enhance mutual understanding of technology and risks send a positive signal, as misunderstandings inevitably stem from speculation and suspicion in the absence of sufficient communication.

What do US interlocutors need to understand about China’s approach to international AI governance ahead of these talks?

China has articulated its stance on international AI governance through the Global AI Governance Initiative, and many of its propositions serve as valuable references. First, the principle of respecting national sovereignty; second, adherence to a gradual approach; and third, proceeding from the perspective of the common security of all humanity.

What should be on the agenda? Is there anything that should be off the agenda?

No topic should be off the table. By raising their respective concerns, both sides can better understand each other’s priorities and lay the foundation for future cooperation. Both China and the United States attach great importance to national security, so risks touching on national security can be discussed within the bilateral framework. Additionally, the call in China’s Global AI Governance Initiative to “work together to prevent and fight against the misuse and malicious use of AI technologies by terrorists, extreme forces, and transnational organized criminal groups” also serves as a suitable entry point.

JIANG Tianjiao (江天骄) is an Associate Professor at the Development Institute of Fudan University. He also serves as Deputy Director of the Center for BRICS Studies and is a Research Fellow at Center for Global AI Innovative Governance at Fudan. His research focuses on emerging technologies and international security.

What is your expectation for the upcoming AI talks between the US and China?

I am cautiously optimistic about the China-U.S. AI dialogue. The positive momentum in China-U.S. relations this year has created a favorable atmosphere for the AI dialogue. Coupled with China’s APEC host-nation diplomacy, both sides are expected to further implement the outcomes of the two heads-of-state summit and launch mechanism-based dialogue. However, AI is indeed at the very frontier of China-U.S. strategic competition and is extraordinarily complex.

What would you consider a “successful” outcome of the talks, and what would count as a disappointment?

I believe that if both sides can follow through on the consensus reached at the September summit and formally establish an AI communication channel or hotline, that alone would be a tremendous success. Other issues will need to be addressed step by step. Conversely, if the two sides fail to establish this communication channel as expected, that could be a negative signal.

What do US interlocutors need to understand about China’s approach to international AI governance ahead of these talks?

I hope the United States will take note of China’s updated AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, which addresses numerous risks including AI cyber, bio, and loss-of-control risks, indicating that China and the United States are actually on the same page when it comes to AI safety. At this year’s WAIC, President Xi’s keynote address also clearly stated that ensuring AI safety is an important component of China’s international AI strategy. Both sides can engage in more dialogues to reduce miscalculations.

YAO Xu (姚旭) is Secretary-General of the Center for Global AI Innovative Governance and an Associate Professor at the Development Institute, Fudan University, among other appointments. He has been recognized as a Shanghai Young Leading Think Tank Scholar and a Young Elite of the Shanghai Municipal Government.

What is your expectation for the upcoming AI talks between the US and China?

We cannot expect one or two rounds of talks to bridge deep structural divergences. A more realistic expectation is establishing a regular, institutionalized communication channel. The primary impediment today is the profound deficit of mutual trust. Therefore, the immediate priority is rebuilding foundational trust through concrete, operational issues, while minimizing extraneous disruptions and actions that erode confidence across related domains. Both sides must transcend zero-sum rivalry and focus on shared technical risks and other potential cooperation. Treating this dialogue as a safety valve against catastrophic miscalculation will provide the cornerstone for stabilizing bilateral relations and gradually exploring incremental cooperation.

What do US interlocutors need to understand about China’s approach to international AI governance ahead of these talks?

First, US interlocutors must recognize that China views development and security as mutually reinforcing. China treats AI safety as an intrinsic capability to enable deployment, not an instrument to constrain innovation. Second, security dialogue cannot be divorced from fairness: demanding unilateral safety commitments amid strict export controls and technological containment is fundamentally unbalanced; Washington should respect Beijing’s legitimate pursuit of dignity and equitable development. Finally, Beijing anchors governance in sovereign equality and inclusive multilateralism. China opposes politicizing technical standards or creating exclusive technology blocs, advocating instead for non-discriminatory, globally shared governance frameworks.

How should this bilateral track relate to multilateral efforts such as the UN Global Dialogue, the Scientific Panel and WAICO?

The bilateral track and multilateral frameworks should form an organic, complementary ecosystem rather than a substitutive one. US-China dialogue serves as a crucial testing ground for consensus and risk containment, but it cannot supplant the UN’s significant role. Both powers must avoid a duopolistic mindset and actively align with the UN Global Dialogue, the Scientific Panel, and WAICO. Based on those multilateral platforms, they should orient discussions toward the Global South’s pressing needs. Actually, it’s better to move past abstract existential risks to prioritize digital infrastructure and capacity-building. Ultimately, bilateral trust must translate into global public goods that bridge digital divides. That will be a significant signal to the world to demonstrate responsibility.

Nvidia’s Friends With Benefits

Trump talked tough about beating China in the AI race while making it easier for his favorite chipmaker to supply the competition.

Nvidia’s Friends With Benefits

Trump talked tough about beating China in the AI race while making it easier for his favorite chipmaker to supply the competition.

Catherine Rampell

READ TO ME

Hi, everybody, welcome to this week’s edition of Receipts.

Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang is out as CEO after what might well have been the most expensive affair in history. I get that the sexy angle is what plays big on TV, but the bigger story is the Trump administration’s decision to sell out U.S. interests. Again. That’s the topic of this week’s newsletter; unfortunately I suspect it may also be the subject of many other newsletters to come.

Got a theory about why the Trump administration, despite its professed China hawkery, remains so lackadaisical about selling frontier technologies to a China-linked company? Leave me a note in the comments.

And if you’re not already a member of Bulwark+, I hope you’ll consider joining our community. There will be lots to track and unpack in the months ahead.

Join Bulwark+ today

–Catherine

(Photo illustration by Bill Kuchman/The Bulwark | Photos: Getty, Shutterstock)

THE MOST SALACIOUS PART of the Nvidia story is the apparent honeytrap that ensnared the company’s founder, Jensen Huang, and ultimately led to his resignation on Thursday.

Yet far more scandalous than Huang’s affair(s) is the apparent coverup by a Trump administration so keen to protect its friends, and so eager to juice the stock market, that it was willing to trade away U.S. interests.

Put another way, the horndog may be the headline. But the real story is the transactional way the Trump administration handles all of America’s economic security.

This is one of the biggest national security scandals in decades. It also could cause serious economic damage, as it undermines our domestic AI industry and boosts China’s. Heads. Should. Roll.

Trump’s “Export Controls” on Chips Look Largely Performative

As you’ve probably heard by now, Huang had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence services believed to be a Chinese spy.¹ The administration knew about Huang being compromised. Donald Trump did, too. The president was warned at least twice, including once right before he picked up Huang on Air Force One en route to Beijing. And yet the administration did nothing.

Actually, worse than nothing: Officials bent U.S. policy to be more favorable to Nvidia and China, and to make it easier for the former to supply the latter.

Why did Trump do that? Charitably, he was persuaded by Huang’s entreaties to loosen export controls on Nvidia’s chip sales to China.² Back in May 2025, for instance, the administration announced it would not enforce and ultimately scrap Biden-era restrictions on advanced-chip exports to many countries, including potential transit points for re-shipments into China. The Commerce Department also appears to have cleared chip sales to companies that may not exist (or that do exist, but are under sanctions).

A MESSAGE FROM OUR SPONSOR CLIMATE POWER

The reckoning is in the receipts.

MAGA leaders blocked cheaper power from wind and solar, rubber-stamped unchecked data center growth, and backed Trump’s war in Iran. Families paid more to fill their tanks and keep the lights on. On Election Day, voters held those leaders accountable. Learn more.

Commerce also halted an investigation into one of those shell companies—Megaspeed, the company formerly led by Huang’s paramour, alleged Chinese agent Alice Huang—apparently after an inquiry from Nvidia. And Commerce declined to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist that would restrict its access to U.S. technology, despite recommendations from the intelligence community and White House officials, based on concerns it was a front for the Chinese government. As of Thursday, Nvidia still lists Megaspeed as a “cloud partner” on its website.

In other words, even as Trump and his lackeys claimed that the United States dare not regulate AI because constraining U.S. tech firms might enable China to “win” the AI race, the administration turned a blind eye to sales of AI-critical chips to an apparent Chinese spy. In many ways, these export controls—first put in place under Trump 1.0 and then expanded under Biden³—had become ornamental.

The question is: Why would an administration populated by purported China hawks look the other way?

Share

Quids, quos, and 关系

We don’t know for sure, but a few pieces of information seem pertinent when answering that question.

Huang has, shall we say, a very cozy relationship with Trump, who continued to praise Huang even after he resigned from the company. Nvidia “donated” $25 million to Trump’s ballroom, tied for the largest amount given.⁴ And in April 2025, Huang attended a $1-million-per-plate candlelight dinner at Mar-a-Lago, where he reportedly persuaded Trump to postpone planned restrictions on chip sales to China.

But even without a seven-figure entrance fee, Huang and Trump kibitzed on the phone all the time, according to reporters who cover Nvidia. Trump likes winners, and until recently, Nvidia was the most valuable company in the world. So Huang was a fun friend to keep around.

Trump also seems to fancy himself as being in business with Nvidia.

You may recall that when Trump gave permission to Nvidia to sell its powerful H200 chips to China, he imposed one big condition: that the United States get a cut. Chips manufactured in Taiwan had to be routed through the United States on their way to China so Trump could collect his 25 percent tariff. As for what became of those chips once they ended up in China, Trump doesn’t appear terribly bothered: He believes himself to be close personal friends with Chinese President Xi Jinping, as well.⁵

Join now

Finally, the AI boom is propping up much of the economy and stock market right now: Ten stocks heavily exposed to AI account for about 40 percent of the entire S&P 500 index’s total market cap. Want to keep the gravy train going? That means keeping the whole sector strong—and the sector in turn critically depends on Nvidia.

Nvidia’s chips are key inputs in data centers around the world. They’re used to train AI models run by the major hyperscalers (Google, Amazon, Microsoft, etc.). And Nvidia’s relationships with other companies in the sector are even more incestuous: The firm is not just a supplier to the troubled AI cloud platform CoreWeave, for instance; it’s also among the largest shareholders and a major customer of CoreWeave, too. This is the “circular financing” you may have heard about. Nvidia has been nicknamed the “central bank” of the AI buildout for good reason. In addition to designing chips, it is guaranteeing leases, backstopping debt, and buying equity stakes in many of the companies it sells to. Even power companies can’t escape Nvidia’s orbit.

The upshot is that Nvidia and Huang had a huge financial interest in being able to sell to more customers, including those in China. But so too did anyone else who might have worried that curbing Nvidia’s sales—or worse, revealing its role in a sexpionage scandal—might destabilize the overall AI industry, and by extension, the overall stock market.

Not that there’s anyone in government who might prize stock-market performance over U.S. security.

Want to comment? Join Bulwark+

Ramparts

— When Huang testifies before Congress later this month—as is now expected—lawmakers need to focus their questioning on conversations he had not just with Trump but with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. If recent reporting is accurate, Lutnick’s behavior could be described as either lazy foot-dragging or outright insubordination. It would also be worth asking why Nvidia abruptly changed how it publicly reported sales so that it no longer disclosed revenue from Singapore. (Megaspeed is a Singaporean company.)

— The Economist suggests this may have been the most expensive affair in history, as it wiped out perhaps a half-trillion dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s market cap.

— The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget has been tracking how well the economic projections from the White House Council of Economic Advisers over the past two years have matched reality. Turns out—you may want to sit down for this—the administration forecasts were on the rosy side.

Share

— Dems’ solution to high house prices is . . . subsidizing demand.

— Beef prices are not coming down anytime soon, either.

— Interesting observation from a new Foreign Affairs article on the “luxury of children”: “Richer and more educated households in the United States and other advanced economies now tend to have more children than poorer and less educated ones, reversing a pattern that had held for centuries.”

— Kalshi has parted ways with Donald Trump Jr., who was a paid adviser to the firm. I interviewed Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour at a recent event at the Economic Club of New York. When I asked him about his company’s relationship with Don Jr., Mansour said the president’s eldest son was hired because he has a large social media following, and the hire was not a “political decision.”

Leave a comment

He also had affairs with at least two Nvidia employees, according to Reuters. Turns out there are some ways that AI already vastly outperforms humans; one of those is in avoiding midlife crises.

Huang’s main argument—also embraced by Trump’s erstwhile AI and crypto czar David Sacks—is that the way to “beat” China is to get the entire world dependent on our tech stack. Which basically means selling as many chips to as many comers as possible, including perhaps in China. The counterargument is that compute is a scarce commodity; cutting-edge American chips are used to train AI models; and we want that training done in the United States, not in China.

Ben Buchanan and Tantum Collins, two Biden administration alumni, released a new book this week that goes over the history of these export controls and other policies influencing the development of AI. It has several chapters related to Nvidia.

The only other corporate “donor” to give that much was Apple. Which might be one reason why Trump wants Tim Apple Cook to take over Nvidia.

NEWSLETTER · 13 Nov 2026, 00:40

The Nvidia scandal escapes containment

Global power is in flux. Your daily guide to what comes next. By RIYA MISRA and CHARLIE MAHTESIAN Welcome to POLITICO Forecast. The team is filling in

Global power is in flux. Your daily guide to what comes next.

By RIYA MISRA and CHARLIE MAHTESIAN

Send tips here | View in your browser

Welcome to POLITICO Forecast. The team is filling in tonight for Jack Blanchard. Drop us a line.

5 THINGS THAT MATTERED TODAY

— U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

— Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid mounting scandals.

— Russia launched attacks on Kyiv, just hours after the Abu Dhabi peace talks concluded.

— President Donald Trump pulled Vice President JD Vance out of his role in Iran negotiations.

— European leaders gathered in Dublin for the European Political Community summit.

THE NEXT NEWS CYCLE

Jensen Huang gives a keynote speech in Berlin on Oct. 21, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

Today, the Nvidia blast radius expanded beyond Wall Street and Silicon Valley to scorch Beijing, Washington and other world capitals.

The events surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation initially triggered financial and market shockwaves because of the chipmaker’s position at the heart of the AI investment boom. Now, the fallout is beginning to reverberate across a different realm — geopolitics and AI policy.

In Washington, the Huang scandal stoked the appetite for oversight of tech executives among Democrats, POLITICO’s Decoded newsletter noted this morning. Even before the latest Huang news, the newly-ascendant Democrats were planning to make Nvidia’s business more difficult — they want to increase export controls on selling chips to China and hold hearings featuring major tech CEOs.

China hawks in both U.S. parties, in fact, have seized on the revelations of Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Key House intelligence Committee lawmakers are urging a probe of the relationship, POLITICO’s Gabby Miller writes this afternoon; among other things, they’re asking intelligence agencies to immediately provide written responses and classified briefings to Congress that includes an assessment of Beijing’s intentions and methods for undermining the U.S. leadership in advanced technology, and a chronology of potential interactions between PRC intelligence and Alice Huang, the alleged spy.

Nvidia’s former CEO has agreed to testify before Capitol Hill lawmakers, though the time and format of his testimony has not yet been worked out.

While Huang may be going through the wringer, Decoded’s Sam Sutton tells Forecast that “Nvidia’s business is still fundamentally sound — at least according to market analysts who study its finances — and there isn’t evidence that its existing financial commitments to the AI growth story are at risk. But the trajectory is going to be different without Huang at the helm.”

“The thing to keep an eye on will be how Nvidia operates as a financial backstop for other AI and AI-adjacent businesses moving forward,” Sam says. “It’s been called AI’s central bank. If Huang’s absence makes it harder for AI companies to finance their future commitments to pay for compute — or if it pushes up borrowing costs across tech-related infrastructure — that’s going to have consequences for the industry’s future growth.”

Still, the scramble to respond to the espionage scandal fallout has, in true Washington fashion, turned to a search for scapegoats — and Commerce Department chief Howard Lutnick and other agency leaders appear to be prime targets to get thrown under the bus.

Reports that Commerce failed to take action on Megaspeed, the Singapore-based firm at the center of the spying and chip-smuggling allegations, have intensified scrutiny of the agency’s decisions and raised questions about whether private tech interests were placed above national security, write POLITICO’s Ari Hawkins, Gabby Miller, Jordain Carney and Katherine Hapgood.

All of it muddies the water in advance of U.S.-China trade talks at next week’s APEC summit, where President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

At the same time, the Huang saga is revealing something else: Europe’s role as a spectator in the global AI race. Pieter Haeck, POLITICO Europe’s senior technology reporter, tells us it is almost fully reliant on the U.S. or China for both the frontier AI models, but also the hardware underpinning those models, such as Nvidia AI chips. While it’s trying to reduce that reliance, that won’t change overnight.

“As a mere customer, Europe has little say over the security implications of this all. Even more so, just last month several European leaders rolled out the red carpet for Huang when he was on a tour in Europe, in a bid to secure supply and investments,” Pieter explains.

One European capital, in particular, will be following the developments closely: Amsterdam.

The Netherlands is the home of ASML, the world’s leading supplier of chip printing machines, with over 60 worldwide locations including in Asia and the U.S. “If the U.S. cracks down on China’s access to advanced chips, that might impact ASML — and the Netherlands, as well,” Pieter says.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“The air of corruption around the Trump administration was very concerning, to millions of Americans.”

— Former U.S. Vice President Mike Pence, who served in Trump’s first White House, rips the current administration in his assessment of Republicans’ midterm losses.

HARD POWER: CANADA STRAINED

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon celebrates his electoral victory on Oct. 5, 2026. | Andrej Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images

Quebec’s separatist leader has forced his way into the Canada-U.S. trade war — creating a crack in Prime Minister Mark Carney’s “Canada Strong” image.

The spat started when Quebec’s newly-elected premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, wrote to 59 U.S. governors and senators from states tied to Quebec — like Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed — pitching closer U.S.-Quebec collaboration on trade and the economy.

Carney, however, chided Quebec’s attempt to take the tariff fight into its own hands: “It’s always a good idea to have one single negotiator,” he told reporters on Tuesday, reminding St-Pierre Plamondon that his government — not the provinces — has final say over trade deals.

But his criticism only made the premier double down: “Mr. Carney is not my boss,” he shot back later that day. “Welcome to Quebec. We have always taken our place.”

It’s not the first tiff between the two leaders. Last month, St-Pierre Plamondon accused Carney of muzzling him by denying him speaking time at the Quebec-hosted Canada-EU summit. He once called Carney “out of line” for discouraging Alberta’s own separatist referendum. And the two still haven’t even met in person.

St-Pierre Plamondon is emerging as one of Carney’s biggest critics, POLITICO Canada’s Mickey Djuric tells Forecast — something “we haven’t seen in Canada yet,” she says. “Carney has been enjoying an unusually long honeymoon and remains deeply popular with voters.”

As Forecast previously laid out, the election of a separatist premier is a big headache for the prime minister, whose central mission is uniting the country in the face of Donald Trump’s aggressive trade war.

“The public clash is becoming harder to ignore,” Mickey tells Forecast. “Ever since the PM was elected, Canada’s premiers have been working tirelessly to maintain a public ‘Team Canada’ image alongside Carney as he negotiates with Trump. As Ottawa tries to secure a deal with Washington, they know any public cracks could signal to Trump that premiers can be played off against the federal government — and each other.”

The two men will meet face-to-face for the first time this weekend, at the Francophonie Summit in Cambodia. Maybe they’ll keep their elbows down.

**Twenty years of POLITICO. One search away. Every fight in politics has happened before, in some form, and we were probably there for it. The new POLITICO app lets you search nearly twenty years of our reporting from your phone, across articles, newsletters, podcasts and people at the same time. Ask about a bill, a minister, a trade dispute or a budget standoff and get the whole story back: what happened last time, who was involved and how it ended. It's the backstory in seconds, wherever you are. Handy before a meeting, essential before a vote, and (we're told) slightly addictive on a long train journey. Get the new app.**

SOFT POWER: A HOUSE DIVIDED

Over 50 European leaders are in Dublin today, digesting the results of this week’s U.S.-mediated Abu Dhabi negotiations — and debating who should represent Europe in future peace talks with Russia.

The problem: Nobody can decide. At least three distinct camps are already forming, POLITICO Europe’s politics reporter Seb Starcevic writes from Dublin, where he reported from the European Political Community summit.

“Some want European Council President Antonio Costa to take the lead,” Seb tells Forecast. “Others — including Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, who I just caught up with — want a seat at the table for the EU’s chief diplomat, Kaja Kallas, one of Europe’s most outspoken Russia hawks. (A European diplomat responded with a long string of “hahahahahas” when I floated that idea.)”

Then there’s Paris and Berlin, Seb adds, “which aren’t particularly keen on having a single person speak for Europe at all.”

Some delegates are souring on the idea of the summit itself, our colleagues report in Brussels Playbook this morning. When French President Emmanuel Macron launched the EPC after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he billed the gathering as a “new space for political cooperation.” But his much-hyped summit hasn’t yielded concrete deliverables in recent years, devolving into more of a glorified meet-and-greet (an exercise in “speed dating,” one diplomat said about last year’s Copenhagen-held summit).

“The whole thing is classic Europe and extremely EU-coded,” Seb says. “In my three-ish years covering politics here, there is always a gigantic list of crises, plenty of palpable urgency to do something about them, but no shortage of (often infuriating) disagreement about how to go about it.”

The discussions will pick back up in Dublin tomorrow, with an informal meeting of the European Council — although it remains to be seen if the bloc’s leaders can find any more common ground. See you Sunday.

WEEKEND AGENDA

— European leaders to hold a second day of strategic meetings in Dublin.

— The October U.S. Producer Price Index will be released Nov. 13.

— French President Emmanuel Macron, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon to attend Cambodia’s Francophonie Summit on Nov. 14 and 15.

— Ministerial meetings to take place in Manila on Nov. 13 and 14 ahead of next week’s ASEAN Summit.

NEWSLETTER · 13 Nov 2026, 00:15

How Will the Iran War End?

Tricky diplomacy and an enduring stalemate. Also: the Global Briefing news quiz, the options on Iran, lame-duck danger, and a suggestion for NATO …

ADVERTISEMENT

Thursday, November 12, 2026 View in browser

Insights, analysis and must reads from CNN’s Fareed Zakaria and the Global Public Square team, compiled by Global Briefing editor Chris Good

Seeing this newsletter as a forward? Sign up here.

How Will the Iran War End?

Just as Vice President (and Iran war opponent) JD Vance was reportedly considering direct talks with an Iranian hardliner to try to end hostilities, President Donald Trump has pulled him off the task of negotiating. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump posted to social media.

This will leave observers even more befuddled as to the fate of the war and the Strait of Hormuz. In a Wall Street Journal op-ed, Gen. David Petraeus (ret.) warns that it matters how this war ends. “A settlement that lets Iran restore its revenue and maritime commerce, continue to threaten navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, rebuild its nuclear program and keep its highly enriched uranium wouldn’t advance American and allied interests,” Petraeus writes. “It would set the conditions for the next crisis.” The US “retains considerable leverage” to extract concessions from Tehran, Petraeus argues, given the effectiveness of America’s blockade on Iranian shipping.

Time will tell. As far as the Strait of Hormuz goes, former US Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for the Middle East Dana Stroul argues in a Foreign Affairs essay for a multinational naval coalition to keep the strait open. Assembling such a force could be difficult, but Stroul notes that Iran would “think twice before attacking a mission made up of dozens of navies all working together.”

More broadly, Iran expert Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations writes hopefully of two alternative diplomatic tracks. US–Iran talks have made little progress since the ill-fated June ceasefire that collapsed in early July. But apart from any American negotiations, top diplomats from a handful of European countries (Britain, France, Germany and Italy) have met with Middle East powers (Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia) to work toward regional stability. High-ranking officials from Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have also met recently with Iranian leaders, Geranmayeh notes.

“These regional powers are scrambling to de-escalate,” Geranmayeh writes, “as Tehran has made clear that its response to renewed US or Israeli strikes would be far more damaging than anything the Middle East has absorbed in the past eight months. … Whether these tracks succeed or fail, they point to a changing reality. Most glaring is America’s absence from both meetings, as European and regional powers increasingly try to work around an unpredictable Washington rather than with it.”

Iran’s nuclear program has bedeviled the US—but it initially began with Washington’s support. Tune in to CNN Sunday night at 8 p.m. ET and PT for Fareed’s latest hourlong special, “Iran and the Bomb,” which explains the complicated history of Iran’s clandestine nuclear program. It’s critical context that helps explain why America is at war today.

a) Extramarital affairs

b) Wiretapping

To see the answer, read to the end of this newsletter.

The Options on Iran

Follow the link below to watch

With the midterms now over, what can the US do to wrap up its war with Iran? On Sunday’s GPS, Adm. James Stavridis (ret.) told Fareed Washington has three options: walk away, resume intense hostilities or make a deal.

Dangerous Times in Trump’s Final Years?

No longer bound by a need to be reelected, Trump can steer US foreign policy in almost any direction he likes. Making world affairs even more unpredictable in the next two years, the political scientist Francis Fukuyama warns at Persuasion that because Trump appears likely to be replaced by a Democrat who will reverse many of his foreign policies, US adversaries have two remaining years to make their moves.

If Chinese leader Xi Jinping “were ever willing to attack Taiwan,” Fukuyama writes, “it would have to be in the next two years. What is the likelihood that a lame-duck Trump would meet a Chinese challenge with a spirited military defense of Taipei? … Trump has essentially switched sides in Russia’s war with Ukraine … A Democratic president in 2029 could reverse this quickly … [Russian President] Vladimir Putin has every incentive to complete the military conquest of Ukraine in the next two years.” The same is true for North Korea, Fukuyama writes: “what is the likelihood that a lame-duck President Trump would take a strong stance in defending South Korea, and commit to using American nuclear weapons as a deterrent against the North? Again, the window of opportunity lies in the next two years, not after.”

Clearly, Fukuyama’s worry is informed by Trump’s current policies and a concern that as a lame duck, the president would be even less willing to defend US allies. But Trump’s final two years in office will be unpredictable for other reasons, too. Trump can remake the world in other ways, depending on how he approaches a packed foreign-policy agenda, Bloomberg columnist Hal Brands writes: “The president must end the Iran war without wrecking America’s position in the Middle East. He faces the unfinished business of peacemaking in Ukraine … He’ll look to consolidate the ‘Donroe Doctrine’—his effort to ensure US primacy in the Western Hemisphere—even as the risk of North American fragmentation looms. The president must also navigate a US-China rivalry that could yet veer in dangerous directions. Finally, Trump has pledged to renew US power by winning the AI competition … How Trump handles these five challenges will define his strategic legacy. It will also determine how messy a world—and how strong a US position—his successor inherits.”

Clusters of NATO

As the US pulls back its once-ironclad commitment to defend Europe against Russia, Matti Pesu of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs argues in a Foreign Affairs essay that the future of NATO might involve the “Nordic model”: neighboring, like-minded NATO members working together within the alliance to confront shared threats in a more concerted manner than the whole of NATO might be inclined to.

The Russia-bordering Baltic countries might consider that paradigm, Pesu argues. So might Turkey and Balkan NATO members. The inspiration comes from the Nordics. Pesu writes: “The Nordic countries have expanded regional collaboration significantly in the past four years. Between them, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden now boast a new long-term defense strategy, a cross-border transit area, frequent joint exercises, and unprecedented levels of command integration. In effect, these governments are forming their own regional deterrence cluster: a like-minded group of states deepening military cooperation to strengthen deterrence and, if required, ensure NATO’s broader collective defense.”

News Quiz: The Answer Is …

Question: Indonesia’s vice president has just resigned, and earlier this month Indonesian officials were arrested, amid a scandal over what? Answer: wiretapping

The story is very complicated, but it involves Indonesian political families and suspicions of betrayal. Indonesia is led by President Prabowo Subianto, whose administration has included figures close to his predecessor, the former president Joko Widodo. Joko’s son has resigned as vice president amid signs of trouble in the alliance between the two camps, the BBC’s Astudestra Ajengrastri and Koh Ewe report.

This comes as Indonesian politics have been rocked by allegations of wiretapping, as The New York Times’ Muktita Suhartono writes: “Earlier this month, what appeared to be a seismic break in the Jokowi-Prabowo alliance emerged. Several officials, including Mr. Prabowo’s chief of staff, who were seen as close to Mr. Joko, were arrested on charges of wiretapping the president.” Erin Cook writes for the Australia-based Lowy Institute’s The Interpreter blog: “Indonesia was jolted last week by accusations that the phones of President Prabowo Subianto and a string of other high-profile figures were illegally wiretapped by a conspiracy within the National Police. The allegations have dredged up a longstanding political rivalry at the heart of recent Indonesian politics between Prabowo and former President Joko Widodo.”

For one thing, the scandal reveals the shakiness of alliances between political families, when cooperation is needed during transitions of power from one to the other. “More generally this will only contribute to the sense that the wheels are coming off for Indonesia,” Foreign Policy’s Joseph Rachman writes. At the Australian ABC News, Tim Swanston and Ari Wuryantama write: “This week, some in Indonesia were describing what’s allegedly occurred in the halls of power as a ‘Watergate’ moment.”

Snapshot of the day

November 12, 2026

Anirudh S.K., Kalrav Joshi

“I have a request for the media,” Prime Minister Narendra Modi told a gathering of journalists in Delhi today. “Communication is the strongest tool in the 21st century and we need to tell the ‘India story’ to the world.” Amen. Well, today’s ‘India story’ is that the Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng, whose pointed (and unrequited) question to Modi earlier this year in Oslo again spotlit his aversion to the press, has said that his government cancelled her Indian visa just before she was to board her flight to Hyderabad for the Congress’s Bharat Summit. Though she was granted political clearance and subsequently a visa to speak about the freedom and future of the media at the event, she was informed at the eleventh hour on Wednesday that her visa’s been cancelled, Lyng said.

But perhaps this is not the India story that the prime minister wants the world to hear. Actually, he was pretty clear that it isn’t: “I request the Indian media to work on the success stories of the country,” he told the gathering in Delhi today. “A lot of such work is already being done.” Allowing Lyng to ask questions in India could have allowed the government to project confidence but maybe its press relations is fated to remain a work in progress for some more time.

As it happens, Lyng was not the only foreign guest of the Bharat Summit to be ultimately denied an opportunity to visit. Over 110 of the 315 speakers whom the external affairs ministry had cleared for the event slated to start Friday ended up being refused entry to India. A source close to the summit’s organisers told The Wire that the government’s FAQs on hosting such events mention only two circumstances under which Indian embassies are required to refer cases to the external or home affairs ministries: when participants hail from China, Pakistan or Sudan, and if the foreigners concerned must visit Jammu and Kashmir or parts of the northeast.

Inventor-activist Sonam Wangchuk says he has virtually been placed under house arrest, with security personnel and vehicles surrounding his residence in Leh for over a day now. He was picked up by police – some of whom wore hoodies and masks but not their nameplates, he says – from his protest site yesterday. Wangchuk’s Leh Apex Body and the Kargil Democratic Alliance had announced protests against hill development council polls being scheduled in the dead of winter; against the abrupt halt in talks with the Union government over constitutional safeguards; and against the lack of a final report into the deadly September 2025 violence in Leh. The authorities have responded by banning protests in the run-up to the elections.

Asaduddin Owaisi and Chandrashekhar Azad have announced an alliance between their Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen and Azad Samaj Party (Kanshiram) ahead of the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections – this is the first outwardly declared front comprising a third one other than the NDA and the INDIA bloc. But Azad said the alliance would be more than just some third front: it is a coalition for social change, he asserted. “As more people from the marginalised, deprived, oppressed, exploited, and downtrodden sections join, this front will become an even more formidable force.” The BJP and CM Adityanath’s principal opponent, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, has welcomed the alliance. “People who used to fall for emotional slogans and deception and vote for communal forces will no longer turn to them … This will cost the BJP another 2–3% of the vote,” he claimed.

For the BJP, the political challenge is that even a relatively small shift in votes could matter in a tightly contested election, particularly if the alliance draws support from Dalit, Muslim and other marginalised communities.

A day after militants opened fire at CRPF jawans in Kashmir’s Kulgam, injuring three of them, the dead bodies of two special police officers were recovered from the upper reaches of the Chenab valley in Kishtwar and contained bullet wounds, reports Peerzada Ashiq. They went missing while accompanying soldiers in the area, where one of the police’s temporary operating bases set up in view of increased militant activity was located. The authorities have not issued a formal statement or confirmed the involvement of militants in the incident.

Air pollutant measurements around Diwali did not really go missing from its online portals but were instead excluded from calculations because they were out of range, the Central Pollution Control Board has claimed. It also sought to justify capping AQI readings at 500 on the grounds that any figure above that would fall within the ‘severe’ category anyway and point to the same health effects. Aathira Perinchery explains all that is wrong with the CPCB’s arguments.

Among the measures Delhi’s government takes when the air turns toxic is halting construction activities. Experts point out that this is not a long-term solution, but there is no end in sight to this practice for now, and in the meantime the city’s construction workers are suffering. No work means no pay, which for some labourers in turn means no meals...

AT THE SCENE

Kyiv, Ukraine

Ukrainians struggle with blackouts

The thought of moving to somewhere safer, or warmer, weighs heavily on Daryna's mind.

US envoys are holding talks with Russian and Ukrainian leaders in Moscow and in Dublin, respectively. On the ground in Ukraine, families are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts due to intensified Russian attacks on their energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking oil refineries in Russia.

Dan Johnson, BBC News

Just before 19:30, there's a click and that's it - darkness until dawn. The lift doesn't work, the water will stop flowing because electricity is needed to pump it to their flat. So the torches and LED candles come out and Daryna, her son Kyryll and daughter Olena gather for a card game of Uno before an early night.

Blackouts sweep entire neighbourhoods, smothering homes and streets in darkness. "You have a big city around but you see nothing because there's no light," Daryna says. Nationwide, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians have gone without power in recent weeks. We saw why on a visit to one of Ukraine's largest power stations.

12 November, 2026

Alex Binley

Hello. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's future at the second-most valuable company in the world may be at risk following new allegations. After the Covid pandemic changed working patterns, find out what's happening to empty offices. And watch as a historic ship sinks.

TOP OF THE AGENDA

Nvidia board reportedly weighs ousting Huang after second affair allegation

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTgsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAByno99D2jS58j7k8wgMFBE680VSsE_-WoNdDJhPhOFHJ1mA47G7kZLGqK_eNMNC9Qnkxg7zEAhb5qMcGFkpHvqcS7O3q_MldyrKxJsp5 Jensen Huang is one of the faces of the global AI boom. Credit: Reuters

Stocks in tech giant Nvidia have plummeted again following reports in the New York Times that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with an executive who reports directly to him. It comes just days after the 63-year-old admitted an affair with another woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. In the wake of the claims, some top investment firms have cut their ratings on Nvidia. The firm's board is reportedly meeting to consider whether to oust the CEO as concerns over Huang's governance grow, but has not released any statements. Since the Covid pandemic and the rise of working from home, many office blocks now sit vacant. This week, the Asia Society Policy Institute assesses what Democratic control of Congress could mean for U.S. Asia policy, examines how Beijing is using Hong Kong to expand China's global financial reach, argues why Trump cannot fall back on old tactics with North Korea should leader-to-leader talks materialize, and unpacks how longstanding territorial disputes and energy competitors in Southeast Asia complicate Beijing's reach in the region.

What the Democratic Congress Means for Asia

The November 3 elections delivered a sweeping rebuke to President Donald Trump and Republican control of Washington, shattering his political coalition and diminishing his influence over the final two years of his presidency. Congress is poised to be far less acquiescent to Trump’s foreign and trade policy than it was during the first half of his second term.

In this week's https://click.e.asiasociety.org/?qs=ABt7ImQiOjUwNTgsInQiOjE3NTY5LCJzIjoxMH0ACgAAAAAGOPXnqspNWdj6op52EehzA1rY6oW9KJzTxxt52gthqM8v5hR7RI82qCRsk11CLQ38-SkA4AtRL2LRoXbWZ4AFgNk3BtAbJnRcHlyGd_4 Asia Policy Brief , Emma Chanlett-Avery and Shay Wester assess what Democratic control of Congress could mean for U.S. Asia policy, with a focus on tariffs, artificial intelligence, and China.
