Hong Kong's Financial Evolution and China's Global Ambitions

In a recent CCA conversation, Diana Choyleva joins Brian Wong to explore how Beijing is transforming Hong Kong into a platform for China’s financial ambitions—and whether a city whose currency remains pegged to the U.S. dollar can help China reduce its dependence on dollar finance. What could this mean for international investors and Washington?

The conversation marks the release of https://click.e.asiasociety.org/?qs=ABt7ImQiOjUwNTgsInQiOjE3NTY5LCJzIjoxMH0ACgAAAAAGOPXnqsyFUw8mqWumV9uYvxyAYyyxbPUFDdFuOdpHybEkjiU3gnX60shVGOBglIesVmCB59cgUb18nAkiqZnx45cJwm5efw9Ysr6vBv0 Hong Kong’s Financial Evolution: China’s Bid to Shape Global Capital Flows, published by the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis in collaboration with Enodo Economics.

Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

The fallout from unfinished diplomacy during Trump’s first term, the COVID-19 pandemic, and global trends such as the sharp escalation in U.S.-Chinese strategic rivalry and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have destabilized the security landscape and created formidable obstacles to peaceful engagement. Meanwhile, North Korea’s continued nuclear and conventional military expansion and the growing support it is receiving from Moscow have strengthened Kim’s hand.

In a recent article for https://click.e.asiasociety.org/?qs=ABt7ImQiOjUwNTgsInQiOjE3NTY5LCJzIjoxMH0ACgAAAAAGOPXnqs4dZzF6fl1EX5zqroQoQB3htLX4kp6lIzx-erDTCKg9MdGOUbmNH605B_CbsH52k_txnYu-7zLDgQBpwqW4OZG0-DsKspBqkKo Foreign Affairs , Stephen Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery argue that President Trump, facing an emboldened Pyongyang, cannot fall back on old tactics should leader-to-leader talks with Kim Jong Un materialize.

https://click.e.asiasociety.org/?qs=ABt7ImQiOjUwNTgsInQiOjE3NTY5LCJzIjoxMH0ACgAAAAAGOPXnqs-bpUreWzKMYZh9MD4cJ3WUDE5a4vcLIz1k7fdjz87FyH7Nl3APdo-sqFi_iJQqAYxERuSPPTeX_ghzKo3QDTEjJ2OA1IjWqrM Learn More

China’s Gray-Zone Strategy: Taiwan Strait and South China Sea Explained

China is expanding its gray-zone activities in the Taiwan Strait and South China Sea, using its coast guard, maritime militia, and other government vessels to advance territorial claims and challenge regional maritime security without triggering direct military conflict. How can Taiwan, Vietnam, and their partners respond?

In a recent discussion, Seng Chen-En and Nguyen Ba Cuong join moderator Lyle Morris to examine China’s evolving maritime coercion. They discuss Beijing’s tactics around Taiwan and disputed waters in the South China Sea, the implications for regional security, and the role of international law, maritime cooperation, and deterrence in preventing escalation.

China's Nuclear Push Meets Southeast Asia's Trust DeficitChina accounts for roughly half of the world’s nuclear reactors currently under construction, but its overseas reactor exports have succeeded only in Pakistan. In Southeast Asia, where Chinese companies already enjoy a substantial presence in clean energy industries, Beijing has yet to secure a commercial reactor construction contract.

In a new article for ThinkChina, Kevin Zongzhe Li and Genevieve Donnellon-May unpack how longstanding territorial disputes and tough energy competitors in Southeast Asia are complicating Beijing's intention to expand its reach in the region.

The Blue Wave Didn’t End the Gerrymandering Arms Race

GOP redistricting backfired, but Dems want to keep drawing.

Joe Perticone • FREE PREVIEW

READ TO ME

Good afternoon, and welcome back to Press Pass. Congress is wrapping up its first full week back in session after the Democrats absolutely bodied Republicans in the midterm elections. Over the last few days, I’ve spent hours idling in hallways and speed-walking across the Capitol chasing down members of Congress to press them for their points of view on important issues. It’s time- and energy-consuming work that’s only possible because of our Bulwark+ members. Contribute to our time and energy supply by upgrading to Bulwark+ yourself today, and we’ll unlock the doors that lead to the deeper reaches of our content storehouse, including exclusive issues of this newsletter (like today’s!), members-only podcasts, and much else.

Join now

Today’s edition goes back to the drawing board—the one that triumphant Dems are thinking about using to continue redrawing congressional maps. Are any lawmakers worried about their own districts getting carved up or the possibility of a Texas-style backfire, as Republicans experienced last week? The members I spoke with conveyed a lot of uncertainty about the future of the redistricting push. To get a comprehensive picture of where things might be heading, I spoke with a broad spectrum of Democrats and Republicans about the issue.

In addition, the right-wing House Freedom Caucus is slouching toward obscurity. It’s not only that their numbers are dwindling; they historically lose influence when Democrats are in the majority. Naturally, the group has laid out a list of demands for the final stretch of the 119th Congress. Lastly, some January 6th rioters are planning another rally next year. Consider yourselves warned. All that and more, below.

(Photo illustration by Bill Kuchman/The Bulwark | Photos: Shutterstock)

I’m afraid I just blue myself

“They messed up in my district,” Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) told me as we stood just outside the Capitol before the afternoon vote series on Wednesday. “They actually made my district more Democratic, and I went up to the speaker and said, ‘Mr. Speaker, do I thank you or do I thank the White House for making my district?’”

Cuellar handily won re-election after Texas Republicans carved up the state’s electoral maps in the summer of 2025 with the goal of creating more districts for their GOP colleagues to win. They did so at Trump’s prompting, and other states followed their lead. The plan, for now, has backfired. In Texas and elsewhere, the Democratic wave caused recently diluted districts to become more competitive, ultimately resulting in colossal Republican defeats and the election of one of the largest Democratic House majorities in modern history. Now Democrats, who over the past two years have redrawn congressional districts in some states they controlled to counteract Republicans’ efforts, are going on offense, exploring ways they can strengthen their own maps by borrowing from the Republican strategy. But some see major downsides and undue risks in this plan. After all, the public won’t give the party a blue wave in every election cycle.

“I didn’t expect this large of a victory on this, but it is something that they have to be careful about,” Cuellar said.

In an interview with WISN, Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley said he would sign legislation ordering the creation of a new map that would theoretically benefit Democrats in the state. As I previously reported, other states, including Virginia, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Maryland, are teeming with Democrats eager to adjust their maps in advance of the next election cycle.

But some of the moderate members with whom I spoke—both Democrats and Republicans—want everyone to lay down their pencils and rulers and implement standards to stop partisan redistricting...

Nvidia and the World Without Jensen

Is NVIDIA Over? Export Controls, RASA, Open Source Implications, Supply Chain Implications, Affair, US Still Dependent On China

Dylan Patel, Doug, Wayne Ma, and Jordan Nanos

Nov 12

Preview

READ IN APP

Jensen Huang is no longer the CEO of Nvidia. Nvidia’s board was investigating Jensen’s conduct and weighing his future at the company he founded, and clearly the conduct issue is real; it is ethically problematic to have relationships with a customer who is a Chinese CCP asset and with multiple subordinates.

Additionally, we believe there is more at play with his resignatiom after only four days. We believe it is directly tied to the vast smuggling of GPUs. Our Accelerator Model tracks every AI chip’s production and destination, and our data shows more than 1.5GW of Nvidia chips, which are restricted, still ultimately ended up in China. This figure doesn’t even include chips that Nvidia created to circumvent US rules, a story we originally broke.

We believe the US intelligence community is a large part of the push to get Jensen out of Nvidia. Specifically, we believe it is likely that RASA or similar legislation, which has already passed the house, will move forward. AI and chip restrictions on China are going to ramp now much faster with the biggest defender Jensen, gone. We are strong believers in some restrictions, but poorly shaped ones are damaging to US interests.

This sort of legislation will have consequences, and we don’t think politicians are thinking them through.

Here are the clear benefits of the current regime where Chinese labs are able to access GPUs remotely:

Profits flow to American companies.

The US can monitor what Chinese labs are doing.

The US can cut off their access to the GPUs through politics or by force almost instantly, if they choose.

American companies such as NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Supermicro, and Dell all depend on Chinese companies in their supply chain.

American companies such as NVIDIA and AMD employ Chinese engineers (who live in China, to be clear) to develop hardware and low-level software for their GPU systems. Without these engineers, we are certain that the user experience for these GPUs would be materially worse than it is today.

American companies, especially the entire startup ecosystem benefit from the open source research that Chinese companies, students and independent researchers publish using these GPUs today.

China is (even slightly) less motivated to use their domestic accelerators.

Innovations from China flow globally through open innovations of wide expert parallelism, OSS kernel libraries: MSA, DeepEP, DeepGEMM, etc.

With that said we do believe in some AI restrictions to China, but those are more shaped like the MATCH Act then RASA.

Maybe biggest of all: open source is under attack. It’s an open secret that Nvidia works directly with the Chinese labs on open source and helping them optimize GPUs and models. These labs utilize Blackwell GPUs, which Nvidia knows. The US open source ecosystem and many startups rely on Chinese AI models. This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone and the China hawks winning.

But the question that matters for shareholders (and the AI supply chain) is a different one: what is Nvidia without Jensen?

Our view is that the company was never built for him not to be there. He was at the helm for 33 years, and even though the board pressured him out (or he “resigned”) Nvidia would still be materially better off with him there instead of gone. The company was uniquely built to suit the man himself. The company without the man might be an entirely different beast. SpaceX and Tesla don't function without Elon, Nvidia doesn't function without Jensen.

One King, 60 Direct Reports

Nvidia’s corporate structure is odd for a company of its size and scale. Jensen has roughly 60 direct reports, according to his public statements. He has said that CEOs should have the most direct reports because those people require the least amount of management and that he doesn’t have one-on-one meetings with them.

But few of them can do things without Jensen. The company is run like a kingdom with one king, with everyone else, regardless of seniority, a peon doing his bidding. Jensen has said that it doesn’t matter who reports to who as their title isn’t related to how important their job is, and it’s one of the reasons why Nvidia is the “smallest large company in the word” and has so much fewer employees – about 42,000 – despite its big market cap. At Nvidia, there is less politics as a result. Jensen has said this flat network empowers employees and allows the company to adapt more quickly because its technology is also moving so quickly.

This is one of the reasons Nvidia moves fast. Once Jensen set a direction, everyone moved on it together. Former employees have told us that product development and engineering often happen until the last minute so the company can change its mind if it needs to. For example, the GB200 design came together a lot closer to the product cycle than probably anyone would have liked, one former executive told us. Jensen has said he wishes he could keep the company in startup mode forever.

The cost of that structure, however, is that Nvidia doesn’t have a deep bench of successors. Look at Nvidia’s website: only five others, two of whom are legal and finance executives, are featured prominently among his reports. Most of his direct reports aren’t trained for the spotlight and are actively discouraged from seeking it. Few leave to become CEOs of other major companies, with Rene Haas at Arm the rare exception. Few at Nvidia get the chance to shine externally because Jensen makes all the big decisions. But much of Nvidia’s executive team doesn’t mind because heavy is the head that wears the crown, and many are happy to stay until retirement age because they’re well paid, treated well, and believe in the mission and their leader.

No One Wants the Job

Colette Kress has been named interim CEO, but Nvidia is looking for a permanent CEO. That cannot be someone with finance background. The obvious internal names being floated to succeed Jensen on the technical side are Ian Buck and Jonah Alben. Buck, who created CUDA out of his doctoral research at Stanford, joined Nvidia in 2004 and now runs the datacenter business as vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing. He is often placed in charge of things while Jensen travels and frequently speaks at conferences.

Alben, who has been at Nvidia since 1997, is senior vice president of GPU engineering and oversees the design of the company’s GPUs. But realistically, no one person can run it all. We don’t think Buck is capable of running the technical hardware engineering side of the house. Alben and others on his team have technical autonomy, but even he doesn’t control the entire chip side, where other senior leaders who handle many major technical and business divisions also report directly to Jensen. Both are amazing but likely not able to exert the supply chain mastery Jensen has.

There is also the question of whether anyone wants to do the job of CEO. An executive told us earlier this year that “Ian would rather die than succeed Jensen and wouldn’t want that job. Jonah is more respected and people say he could, but again, no one would really want that job.” Circumstances, though, have obviously changed. Kress is the interim CEO, but wrangling more than 60 VPs to a cohesive vision of the company takes a certain kind of person, and otherwise the firm’s direction risks dissolving into noise.

Founder Bets Do Not Survive Professional Managers

Jensen is one of the last old-school tech founders, of the same generation as Elon Musk and a bit older than Mark Zuckerberg. The other companies that came up alongside Nvidia have all transitioned to professional managers, including AMD, Google, Microsoft, Apple and Amazon.

Nvidia’s success relies on big bets that can take years, if not a decade, to pay off. A founder with the full support of the board can take those risks without worrying about a revolt. CUDA lost money for years while Wall Street analysts kept questioning it, but Jensen held steady and the bet paid off enormously. As one former employee put it: “Jensen put the whole company behind programmable shaders, CUDA and tensor cores despite a lot of opposition to spending transistors on them when use was limited.”

Omniverse and autonomous driving are the new bets within Nvidia. Internally, Jensen calls them “zero billion dollar bets,” former employees tell us. They make no money today, but he sees them as just as big as CUDA. He also built the Shield TV consumer entertainment box and the DGX Cloud service on the idea that Nvidia needs to understand its customers to design better products, even if those two businesses made little or no money and were ultimately cast aside.

An Nvidia successor who isn’t the founder, no matter how long they have been at the company, answers to the board and shareholders in a different way. Long-term bets and convictions of this kind become much less likely, and one of the biggest issues is Jensen’s legendary kingmaking and dealmaking, which is going to be hard to replicate.

Customers Bought Jensen, Not Just GPUs

Jensen was the chief decider on chip allocation to the hyperscalers and everyone else. Customers are always jockeying for allocation and fighting for Nvidia’s attention, and more and more of Nvidia’s deals require extensive Nvidia support. As we wrote in July, Nvidia has a choice over whether to allocate more capacity to hyperscalers, neoclouds or neoclouds on its backstop program, where it credit-supports the cluster and takes a share of the cloud revenue. This central bank of Nvidia was backed by the full faith and credit of Jensen. The next CEO is unlikely to be able to make the bold bets Jensen did.

Nvidia likes to decide based on what’s feasible, but much of it comes down to what makes strategic sense. It doesn’t always make strategic sense to skip the hyperscalers, or to work with them and treat them preferentially. Many of these customers now need reassurances that they will continue to be supported by Nvidia through financial guarantees or allocation. Nvidia disclosed $530B of gross off-balance-sheet guarantees as of its fiscal second quarter, up from $184B the prior quarter, including $36B of take-or-pay floors under neocloud capacity, and it holds a $99B equity book.

Many customers also want a deal with Jensen for reasons that go beyond the numbers. Neoclouds around the world raised their money because Jensen backed them, not because they compared chips and chose Nvidia. Nvidia’s backstops let neoclouds and neolabs raise money without the hyperscalers: it sells GPUs at full margin on day one, then floors the buyer’s revenue, guarantees the buyer’s landlord or signs the lease itself, so that operators without an investment-grade rating can borrow at investment-grade pricing. If the Jensen put is not there, there might be a large contraction in this ecosystem.

The Supply Chain Stranglehold Loosens

Nvidia has a stranglehold on its suppliers. If competitors had access to supply, they would ship much higher volume. They can’t get it because Jensen has personally locked up memory in South Korea and chips in Taiwan. As we wrote in The Great AI Silicon Shortage, Nvidia has locked in most of the supply for logic wafers, memory and various other necessary components, and Jensen’s 2025 trip to Korea was to secure memory supply, before other executives quite realized how in shortage memory was. Our industry clients thought our forecasts for 2026 were too aggressive, but then they realized we were right. Nvidia’s supply and capacity commitments jumped from $119B to $279B in a single quarter, primarily for memory.

That stranglehold is personal. Jensen was the one who won these deals, CEO to CEO, with the major supply chain companies around the world. In Korea, we estimate SK Hynix’s 2027 HBM4 pricing could range from roughly $3.0 to $3.3 per Gb for Nvidia versus $3.7 to $4.1 per Gb for other Tier 1 customers including AMD, Broadcom, Amazon and Google, and we believe there is an implicit understanding that Nvidia gives SK Group priority GPU allocation in return. Without him, these firms will no longer prioritize Nvidia to the same degree, and capacity will be easier for others to acquire. We think it’s likely that in 2028 more than 70% of total capacity could be non-Nvidia.

What’s more, beyond strangling the supply, Jensen’s vision is what pushed the supply chain in Taiwan to invest harder and believe more in this buildout than anyone else. Jensen’s legendary supply chain dinners and commitments are what pushed suppliers in Taiwan to deliver on technologically and logistically aggressive plans.

The AI Industry Loses Its Open Source Spokesman

Without Jensen, the AI industry loses its chief spokesman. He was everywhere, speaking on AI as its chief proponent. He was the face of AI, and no one can replace that.

Jensen also set Nvidia’s China policy and led its push for open source AI models, which give countries, enterprises and neoclouds a reason to buy GPUs beyond the handful of frontier labs, who are now building their own chips.

As we wrote in September, no one needs open source AI more than Nvidia: it is on track for a world where it has only two real customers, Anthropic and OpenAI, or seven including the hyperscalers, and all seven except SpaceX are trying to build their own XPUs to cannibalize Nvidia’s margins. AI models and applications are the complements to its GPUs.

It is an open secret that Chinese frontier labs use Blackwell GPUs & NVIDIA DevTech collaborates closely with the Chinese frontier labs & learns a lot from their end users, which results in innovations to the CUDA ecosystem like wide expert parallelism, DeepGEMM, DeepEP etc. These then spread to the western open source community and startups. These startups are massively negatively impacted by the departure.

Without Jensen being the spokesperson and offering financial and engineering help for open models, Chinese labs may not be able to open source kernel libraries like MiniMax MSA, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, Moonshot’s FlashKDA, which are clearly targeted at NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. Many production engines used widely across the world like SGLang & vLLM use these innovations from Chinese labs. Chinese labs may have to go back to straight up denying that they have any NVIDIA GPUs and keep their NVIDIA software internal only instead of open sourcing Blackwell software.

This is fundamentally bad that innovations from China won’t be shared across the NVIDIA ecosystem & the general ML ecosystem anymore. It is positive for closed AI labs but bad for startups.

A manager lead company could depriortize underperforming Nemotron, With many models going closed source at the frontier labs in the U.S., Nvidia was single-handedly propping up the other American open source models with its efforts by investing in firms like Reflection, Thinking Machines, Poolside, and the Hugging Face acquisition.

Nvidia was the one pushing continuous engagement with China, on the argument that China should use and rely on American technology. As we wrote last year, after the U.S. government banned the H20 from going into China and then indicated Nvidia would be granted a license to export it, the U.S. needs to balance having China on the U.S. AI stack and slowing the development of its own, while also limiting the quality and volumes shipped into China. Now, what if he was pushing it from a compromised place? That is up to the investigation to figure out. Clearly the China hawks are winning, so we have to ask a bit of an odd question. Why now?

Why Now Does Jensen’s Personal Life Come to Light?

We aren’t ones for conspiracy theories, but a few events around the same time seem to create a narrative that is hard to ignore. The intelligence community had much to gain. The second New York Times story on the topic explicitly states (five times) that the basis for its reporting is the U.S. intelligence community. Trump, Rubio and Lutnick have known about all of this since before their trip to China in May. What’s more is that there is reporting that Lutnick stalled the Chinese chip crackdown. Something has shifted in that relationship, and now the wind is blowing in the other direction.

We actually don’t believe Alice Huang is a spy in the traditional sense. She is a well connected business woman. She like any other well connected business person in China, has contact with the CCP.

Our Accelerator Model has tracked over 1.5GW of Nvidia GPUs that shouldn’t be in China, The Department of Commerce now also finally believes that there is more than 1.5GW of NVIDIA chips in China that shouldn’t be there. Now, with the midterms swinging the Democrat’s way, someone has decided it is time to put the hammer down both to stop the willing circumvention of the existing export controls and to expand them to cut off China’s access to frontier chips once and for all.

To be clear, the Trump administration is split on the issue, but Trump was giving Lutnick cover. Trump is no longer providing that cover. What’s more, there is a critical bill called the Remote Access Security Act (“RASA”) that has passed the House that has yet to receive a vote in the Senate, and that vote is happening right now.

RASA Up for a Vote

RASA passed the House 369-22 on Jan. 12. It passed on a motion to suspend the rules, which requires a two-thirds majority. The House Foreign Affairs Committee approved it 51-0 in April 2025. Though it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, it hasn’t yet received a vote. We know that NVIDIA and Oracle have been lobbying against it, hard.

Of course, RASA isn’t the only way that the U.S. government can stop Chinese companies from accessing GPUs remotely. But RASA is the bill that is the hot topic of discussion in Washington right now. It is clearly popular, having already passed the House, and the substantive portions of the bill seem downright obvious to people. Why allow Chinese companies to access GPUs remotely that they aren’t allowed to import?

For what it’s worth, we are aware of neoclouds in Asia, Australia, the Middle East, Nordics, Europe, Canada and even the U.S. that are actively selling capacity to Chinese companies. All of them would be impacted by this bill. This is another global export control bill, and one with far-reaching implications. Jensen, and likely Lutnick, did not want this to happen.

So let’s go against the popular narrative and explore the possibility that despite all of the recent headlines, passing RASA (or something like it) will have unintended consequences. To follow the old adage about American politics, we believe that if all the politicians agree on something, it’s probably a bad idea.

As we stated earlier, here are the clear benefits of the current regime where Chinese labs are able to access GPUs remotely:

Profits flow to American companies.

The US can monitor what Chinese labs are doing.

The US can cut off their access to the GPUs through politics or by force almost instantly, if they choose.

American companies such as NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Supermicro, and Dell all depend on Chinese companies in their supply chain.

American companies such as NVIDIA and AMD employ Chinese engineers (who live in China, to be clear) to develop hardware and low-level software for their GPU systems. Without these engineers, we are certain that the user experience for these GPUs would be materially worse than it is today.

American companies benefit from the open source research that Chinese companies, students and independent researchers publish using these GPUs today.

China is (even slightly) less motivated to use their domestic accelerators.

Innovations from China flow globally through open innovations of wide expert parallelism, OSS kernel libraries: MSA, DeepEP, DeepGEMM, etc.

To be clear: in a world where Chinese labs are completely cut off from accessing NVIDIA GPUs, they would all be even more motivated to move off of NVIDIA GPUs and onto domestic accelerators.

Which is already happening today.

In February, Z.ai claimed inference support for GLM-5 on seven domestic accelerators

In April, DeepSeek published their V4 paper and later open-sourced an inference megakernel for the V4 Pro model on Huawei Ascend NPUs.

In June, Meituan claimed LongCat 2.0, which claimed that it was pretrained entirely on Huawei Ascend 910B NPUs.

Source: GLM-5 Paper from Z.ai

Politicians continue to miss how intertwined the China <> Taiwan <> US relationship actually is. Many Chinese nationals work at the frontier labs. Many Chinese engineers are employed by NVIDIA and AMD, writing low level code to bring up new chips. Many Americans learn from Chinese open source contributions. Many of the raw materials needed to produce these chips come from China. Many of the L1-6 ODM board and component suppliers are Chinese.

Escalating tensions will guarantee that less chips are produced, and the pace of AI progress slows for everyone.

We believe the US should limit or control how much comprue is delivered to Chinese labs, and banning export to China while allowing remote access by trusted clouds is a the best method to do this.

Export Control Violations and Enforcement

For all those who say that there is no way GPUs can be smuggled into China and advertised for rental on rednote because they’re too heavy to fit in a backpack, we disagree.

Source: ads on Rednote for an 800 GPU cluster of RTX 5090, and another for a 1,024 GPU minimum purchase in China.

“We’ve studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one. There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion. These are massive systems. The Grace Blackwell system is nearly two tons, and so you’re not going to be putting that in your pocket or your backpack anytime soon. The important thing is that the countries and the companies that we sell to recognize that diversion is not allowed and everybody would like to continue to buy Nvidia technology.” - Jensen Huang at Computex in May 2025

Since then, we have at least two high profile counter examples: $2.5B worth of servers being smuggled by 3x people at Supermicro, and $65M worth being smuggled by 9x people at NVIDIA, Supermicro, Albatron, Flying Tiger, and Chief Telecom (a Taiwanese distributor, reseller, and datacenter operator).

The first $2.5B story is about Wally Liaw, a co-founder of SuperMicro and their Head of Sales. Wally was indicted on March 17, 2026 (US v. Liaw, 1:26-cr-00100, SDNY) along with Steven Chang (Head of Sales for Taiwan) and Willy Sun (local Taiwan contractor). The indictment states that $2.5B worth of servers were sold to a company in Southeast Asia that then $510M were smuggled into China. It also claims that Wally, Steven and Willy staged dummy servers to pass a company audit in Aug 2025, and a Commerce Department audit in Dec 2025.

The indictment literally includes a picture of Willy Sun and his friend using a hair dryer to move labels and serial number stickers from real servers to dummy servers so they could pass an audit.

Source: https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.660027/gov.uscourts.nysd.660027.2.0.pdf

Source: https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.660027/gov.uscourts.nysd.660027.2.0.pdf

Since the indictment in March:

Wally has pleaded not guilty and goes to trial on March 29 next year (it was set to start on Nov 2, but was delayed after Supermicro was subpoenaed by SDNY, as they stated in their 10-K, filed Aug 31)

Willy has pleaded guilty to four counts, including staging the dummy servers, posing as a legal assistant named Michael, lying to the Commerce Department officer in Dec 2025 during their audit, and deleting an encrypted messaging app from his phone the day he was arrested (Mar 19). He pleaded guilty on Oct 8, and sentencing is set for Sep 8 next year.

Steven is currently considered a fugitive.

Source: Supermicro’s 10-K from August

Moving on to the second case in Keelung, Taiwan. 9 people have been indicted (so far) for smuggling 130 B300 servers, with 74 reaching China earlier this year:

Chang Teng-lung, Senior Manager NVIDIA Taiwan (key figure)

Lin and Wang, Sales Managers at Supermicro Taiwan

Lu, CEO of Albatron, a Supermicro distributor

Chen, President of Flying Tiger, a server reseller

Tsai, Project Manager at Chief Telecom, a datacenter operator

Yu, head of a customs clearance company

Wang #2, Head of a server reseller company

An unnamed 9th defendant who siphoned money from Albatron

As the story goes, the Taiwan Coast Guard came across the servers during a drug-smuggling investigation in May and detained three people. They then searched 12 more locations, and seized 56 servers, luxury cars, and NT$9M (about $275k USD) in cash.

Following this, the people from Supermicro, Albatron and Chief Telecom were indicted in June, they got Chang from NVIDIA in July, and by August they had all 9. The first hearing for Chang was held on Oct 16.

The defendants are accused of using shell companies, faking the audit, forging documents (including a mockup of a Supermicro website for export permits), and declaring the exports for Japan, where they would be shipped on to China.

For what it’s worth, current process on orders above eight servers triggers an onsite inspection by Supermicro. The coast guard’s inspection apparently found the servers by chance, while pursuing an unrelated drug-smuggling case. This inspection happened after Flying Tiger had applied and received a license to purchase 130 servers from Supermicro in Sep 2025 with themselves named as the end user, and passed an onsite inspection at a Chief Telecom datacenter. The inspection was supposed to confirm they had enough rack space and power to fit the servers, but prosecutors claim it’s obvious that the site doesn’t meet these requirements. They didn’t even have a lease signed.

Here is a picture from the indictment showing Supermicro servers on pallets with crime scene tape around them, cash, and a porsche

Source: Keelung indictment

Source: Keelung indictment

Both of these cases are being litigated.

It’s Likely Worse Than We Thought

So, if we had to say “why now,” it’s likely to remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill: after a large shift in Congress and heading into a lame duck session, it’s best to get your opposition out of the way to get the bill passed. That is our best conspiracy theory take on the situation, and it lines up with the ripples from Washington. So now let’s return to our original question.

What Does Nvidia Look Like Without Jensen?...

Hello. This week in 1985, US President Ronald Reagan and his wife Nancy welcomed Prince Charles and his young wife Princess Diana to the White House. Below, you'll find an original radio script showing how the BBC reported on the historic visit (and a brilliant photo of the Princess of Wales slow-dancing with the president). Also in this edition is a look at how English bookshops sold out of "obscene" novel Lady Chatterley's Lover at super-speed. But first, did the legend of Jack the Ripper obscure the murderer's true identity? Find out more below.

VIDEO FROM THE ARCHIVE

'The murders were turned into fiction'

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTgsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABy55BQOko-3pyMGCbmBPde0VFHOUdQE0uDGRZiEhDrNWU6G4R1ek4kKR6P_FPD9vXWqA3bu6indeO-TUlsOFuLKkjPP0pHBC60UXPzbJ Did the 19th Century British tabloid press create the mythology of Jack the Ripper? Credit: Getty Images

This week in 1888, Jack the Ripper's fifth and final victim was murdered in east London. The killer was never identified and, even today, the crimes remain unsolved.

Playing in the city's West End at the time was a production of The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. A year earlier, Sherlock Holmes had made his first appearance. Around the same period, an influential London newspaper editor called WT Stead was experimenting with a new sensationalist style that would become known as tabloid journalism.

It was in this context that the Ripper's series of savage murders would move from historical fact to the realms of legend - the subject explored a century later by a BBC documentary. Learn more and watch archive clips from 1988's Timewatch: Shadow of the Ripper via the button below.

FIRST DRAFT OF HISTORY

The US welcomes Charles and Diana

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTgsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABy55BQOsrv4FQVqmz5UwtegrSdbFkjhZ4y5-DcpLsnU9Na2nPk5YnXN0TNM18jNlS79WIGGevZ_rLCiKq4hslfjnGUQWAS1ni1vG44aK Princess Diana dances with US President Ronald Reagan, while First Lady Nancy Reagan dances with Prince Charles, during a White House gala dinner on 9 November 1985. Credit: Alamy

This week in 1985, Princess Diana and Prince Charles (now King Charles) made their first joint visit to the US, where they spent time with President Ronald Reagan and his wife Nancy.

The highlight of the tour was a gala dinner at the White House on their first evening in Washington, where a 24-year-old Diana danced with the actor John Travolta (and President Reagan, as pictured above). Other A-listers were in attendance, including Clint Eastwood, Tom Selleck and the singer Neil Diamond, who supplied the evening's main entertainment.

"The President sat next to the Princess, but he stumbled over her name at the beginning of his public remarks, calling her first Princess David, and then settling for Princess Diane," reported BBC radio on 10 November 1985. "He may have been distracted by the stunning evening dress of midnight blue velvet she was wearing."

Read more about the historic royal visit - described by the BBC as "the most talked about social event Washington has known for many a year" - in the original radio script shared below.

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTgsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABy55BQOtHE4qzmaGFG1DxDnRkfMyx-g31GOH_Cs3SiM7B40XSMkOWINAMYtq0uOfvhTf1KqjPpPd2iB83q4p4QTalbKHpEWI8SmlES66

WHAT HAPPENED NEXT

A packed itinerary

After their White House welcome, the royal couple were taken to the official home of the British Ambassador at the time, Sir Oliver Wright, where they were staying.

Their packed itinerary over the next few days involved visits to a morning service at Washington Cathedral, the National Gallery of Art, Arlington National Cemetery and, rather surprisingly, to a suburban shopping mall in Springfield, Virginia.

Although the royal pair presented a united front during the US visit, their marriage was in serious trouble at the time - and the couple separated in 1993.

In the decades since the 1985 trip, King Charles has continued to make regular official visits to the US, including as recently as April this year. "I was a teenager living in Auckland when the bombing took place," wrote Derek Walker in New Zealand. "My friends and I took a bus into the city the following day, just to have a look. The scene and outpouring of outrage once it became clear that it had been a bomb and not a tragic accident will stay with me. The bombing had the opposite effect that was intended; it woke up a large portion of New Zealand's population. Fernando did not die in vain."

Anthony Clark in Ontario, Canada, shared this memory related to Laika the Russian space dog: "I was 10 when little Laika, as she became known, made her historic flight. It was another Soviet space coup, to be followed by Yuri Gagarin. She was the talk of our neighbourhood, but no one intimated she might not return."

NEWSLETTER · 12 Nov 2026, 18:02

No MFF, no Christmas

Also, in tonight’s edition: Europe's continued struggle over who should talk to Russia

VIEW IN BROWSER

By Victoria Becker

Supported by

When it comes to festive wishlists, forget Santa, speculoos, trees, gifts or tangerines because Christmas is cancelled unless European leaders give António Costa an EU budget deal in the coming weeks.

It is official. The European Council president has told the EU’s heads of state and government that he will cancel all festivities and keep them penned up inside the unChristmassy Europa building until they give him the ultimate gift: an MFF for 2028 to 2034.

Nikos Christodoulides, the Cypriot president, revealed Costa’s threat to Grinch the season’s celebrations today in response to an interview with his Lithuanian counterpart Gitanas Nausėda in Rapporteur.

“He [Costa] told us that when we meet in December, there is no leaving and there will be no Christmas until and unless we have the budget decided and ready,” he told the Cyprus Mail, referring to the summit that begins on 17 December.

His remarks came in reply to President Nausėda downplaying the Christmas deadline, telling us that it was not “terribly fundamental”, as long as a deal was reached by 4 February next year.

Christmas still has a chance. There are still five weeks to go until the December summit.

Tomorrow, EU leaders gather in Dublin for an informal summit, with AI topping the agenda. They are then back in Brussels for a special MFF-themed summit on 26 and 27 November.

On 21 November, Costa will share a new “nego box” as the basis for talks. The ultimate showdown is expected to be in December, a week before Christmas.

Will Costa’s festive wish come true? Like so many presents, the costs can be high.

Too high, perhaps, for the six or so “frugals”, who want to cut the price. Not generous enough, quite possibly, for the 17-strong “friends” of high spending.

Much will depend on how much festive cheer and willingness to compromise there is around the summit table (will there be a special seasonal menu or Glühwein to get them into the mood?) before Costa can declare a “merry Christmas”.

Round-up

MIGRATION EXCLUSIVE: European governments are formally being asked to consider a “broad review” of the EU’s migration and asylum rules next year, potentially paving the way for changes barely six months after the new system began applying, Rapporteur can reveal.

META MOOD UKRAINE: EU leaders are seemingly so divided that they cannot even agree on whether the discussion is on whether Europe should talk to Russia – let alone who should represent it. The topic is expected to be a key point of discussion when the 27 congregate tomorrow for an informal summit.

BONDS SPELL TROUBLE: Tremors in the European bond market could spell trouble for the wider European economy if EU capitals fail to introduce reforms to boost productivity, the IMF’s Europe chief warned on Thursday.

ISRAEL PETITION: A petition to suspend the EU’s association agreement with Israel has received more than a million signatures, forcing the Commission to either table a proposal within six months or explain why it will not do so.

CLIMATE COURT: The EU’s highest court rejected seven lawsuits from Poland’s former nationalist government seeking to scrap EU legislation designed to help the bloc meet its carbon emissions reduction targets – much to the glee of Green MEPs and civil society groups.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/b6eadbff-adf5-41c0-8bbb-d06ab7b84e00/embeddable_95930881-5aaa-4e69-bb35-a3dfa7279a0f.jpg?t=1784735137) Caption:

**Good afternoon.**

In this edition, our contributors examine the gap between a technology’s promise and its real operational utility. A biotech executive and research scholar argue that biomanufacturing could ease the military’s logistics problem if the Pentagon backs a coordinated strategy rather than individual technologies. An Air Force Academy professor and a cadet physicist look past the headlines to make the case for quantum magnetometry. In a follow-up article, two physicists warn that Golden Dome could prove escalatory, whether or not it even works. A former Defense Innovation Unit analyst and the unit’s first warfighter-in-residence argue that the Pentagon’s acquisition overhaul depends on the servicemembers it continues to neglect, and propose a weapons school model to train and support them. And in two separate episodes of the podcast, the editor-in-chief of the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists discusses how Silicon Valley’s defense newcomers are becoming the next primes, and a supply chain CEO, a senior Army financial official, and a retired Air Force general weigh what it will take to rebuild America’s munitions arsenal.

College Republicans Revolt Against Trump

A coalition of student GOP groups blames the president for betraying America First—but look who’s really shaping their politics.

Will Sommer • FREE PREVIEW

READ TO ME

Welcome back to False Flag! Donald Trump’s agenda is in the dumps. Democrats have him on the run. So it’s no surprise that the pro-Trump QAnon conspiracy theory that has always imagined Trump as most powerful when his political condition looks most dire appears to be enjoying a resurgence.

QAnon launched in 2017, amid Robert Mueller’s investigation into Russia’s election meddling. Now it’s returned to once again give succor to Trump supporters. Explanations of the “Q plan” are going viral. The QAnon-style theory that Trump only allowed the blue tsunami so he could catch Democrats stealing elections is taking off among disappointed conservatives.

It’s not just me noticing the Qsurgence. Alex Jones, a onetime QAnon ally who abandoned the conspiracy theory after it threatened to eclipse him, grumbled on his show Wednesday that QAnon is back, calling Trump’s outreach to QAnon “very, very sad.”

“Bare minimum, the White House knows all they’ve got left is Q supporters, that’ll buy anything,” Jones said.

Last time QAnon got big, its believers stormed Congress! We’ll see how QAnon 2.0 shakes out.

But while Trump may still have QAnon in his corner, he’s bleeding supporters somewhere else: among extremely online young College Republicans. Unfortunately, they want to replace Trump with something even worse! That’s the topic of today’s newsletter. You don’t need a college degree to read it, but a Bulwark+ subscription will do. Snag one here:

Miss nothing! Join Bulwark+!

–Will

(Photo illustration by Bill Kuchman/The Bulwark | Photos: Shutterstock)

FEW COMMENTATORS ON THE RIGHT have been willing to blame Donald Trump for last week’s blue wave, choosing instead to castigate everyone from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to now-former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles for their party’s failures.

But a large alliance of College Republican activists has shown no such compunction. Instead, they’re leaning in on calling out the president, even uniting chapters across the country to do so.

In a statement issued the day after the election, a previously little-known group of College Republican chapters calling itself the College Republican Patriot Coalition blamed Trump for abandoning his MAGA principles, not fulfilling his campaign promises, and driving the party off a cliff.

“On all fronts, the Republican Party and the Trump administration in particular has betrayed us,” the open letter reads.

College Republican Patriot Coalition

@CRPatriots

America First is the ONLY way forward. Official CRPC statement on the results of last night's midterm election:

11:12 PM · Nov 4, 2026 · 197K Views

174 Replies · 761 Reposts · 5.95K Likes

The group claims to represent numerous College Republican chapters, many of them from large state universities like the University of Illinois, the University of Florida, and the University of Virginia. The signatories also include College Republican groups in Maryland, Georgia, New York, and other states.

The world of College Republicans can be murky, since there’s no singular body that controls all the college and university chapters. Still, given that the young Republicans likely make up much of the pool of future staffers and conservative operatives, the idea that so many College Republicans would openly challenge Trump—calling for a “purge” of the administration and a new “champion”—has caused a stir.

The open letter listed a number of grievances these College Republicans have with the administration. But one was mentioned twice: Israel, which the group argues convinced Trump to enter the Iran war. The inclusion of those lines might make you wonder if there’s a connection between these College Republicans and white nationalist podcaster and groyper king Nick Fuentes.

Congressional Testimony | One Year Later: Assessing Nigeria's Efforts to protect Christians and Secure the Middle Belt

Thursday, November 12, 2026

11:00 AM -1:00 PM ET

Livestream

Watch Here

On Thursday, November 12th, Rep. Chris Smith (R-NJ), Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Africa Subcommittee, will chair his fourteenth congressional hearing on the religious persecution of Christians by radical Islamist groups in Nigeria, as well as the Nigerian government’s efforts to mitigate the violence and protect vulnerable communities in the Middle Belt.

This congressional hearing will assess the current state of religious violence perpetrated by radical Islamists, such as Boko Haram and Fulani terrorists, against Christians in Nigeria; the Nigerian government’s efforts to curb the persecution and punish those responsible for committing atrocities against Christian and non-radical Muslim communities; and the steps the United States can take to ensure that Nigerian officials are addressing and preventing the systemic violence against Christians and non-radical Muslims by Islamist extremists.

Drawing on her recent trip to Jos in Plateau State, Oge will argue that while Christians in the Middle Belt have suffered horrific violence, religion alone cannot explain the wider security crisis. Lasting protection depends on state capacity, accountability, and early warning that leads to early action. She will also offer recommendations for Congress and the Nigerian government, including how to measure success. This testimony will address the added urgency of conflict prevention ahead of Nigeria’s January 2027 elections.

Headlines & Launches

What's new in Grok Bot 1.0 (11 minute read)

Grok Bot 1.0 adds Team Bots you can publish and share, Slack and Microsoft Teams, meetings on Meet and Zoom, shared connectors, and reviewed learnings. It is now a personal assistant that the whole team can talk to in the app, in Slack, in Microsoft Teams, and in video calls. This post covers how to create a Team Bot and publish it, how to bring the bot into Microsoft Teams, how to add a bot to a meeting, and more. It also looks at the new admin controls and what's possible without a team.

Gemini Decisions API: Fast, calibrated multimodal decisions (1 minute read)

Google's Gemini Decisions API enables fast, calibrated multimodal decision-making by analyzing inputs like images and text. It assesses scenarios and provides actionable insights, such as determining spill severity and recommending cleanup actions.

Runway Praxis-1 Is Now Available: Open-Weight Robotics Model (3 minute read)

Runway's Praxis-1, a 27B-parameter open-weight robotics model, is now available under Apache 2.0. The model excels in predicting video and actions, topping NVIDIA's RoboLab-120 leaderboard with a 46.2% success rate across 1,200 episodes. It's accessible on GitHub and Hugging Face, with support for full and LoRA fine-tuning, compatible with NVIDIA hardware, and adaptable for various robotic embodiments.

Deep Dives & Analysis

MCP vs CLI vs Skills: What Each Costs in Context (11 minute read)

MCP servers significantly increase token use, adding thousands of input tokens per request, unlike CLI or skill methods. On Sonnet 5.5, a simple task showed MCP consuming 59,417 tokens with default tools against CLI's 1,421 and skill's 3,315, highlighting the high cost of tool-heavy MCP setups. Implementing Tool Search can cut token costs by deferring tool definitions, reducing upfront toolset costs to under 600 tokens for optimal efficiency.

Don't Write Kernels, Derive Them (63 minute read)

Current models rely on hand-written kernels specific to operators, chips, and fusions, limiting flexibility across devices and scenarios. Tang's IR enables on-the-fly derivation of kernels through constructs such as views and comprehensions, eliminating the need for pre-defined kernels.

Escaping SPACE: Part II (28 minute read)

Perplexity tested 12 models against its SPACE agent sandbox: none escaped VM-host isolation, but several bypassed network controls through DNS spoofing and shared-IP exploitation before the flaws were fixed. The experiments also found that capture-the-flag prompts distracted agents from the security boundary being tested.

LLMs can learn some multi-step reasoning on filler tokens instead of visible CoT (9 minute read)

By changing the training setup and applying LoRAs to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and gpt-oss-20b, researchers taught models to do some multi-step tasks while emitting only filler tokens, beating an answer-only baseline on three of seven tasks. They also mapped theoretical layer-depth limits and showed empirical walls, with some tasks learned out to 60 steps and others failing after one to three. The work is meant to separate filler-token reasoning from steganographic hidden reasoning when interpreting chain-of-thought.

Users get the same low latency, high trust, and complete native fidelity whether they reach a company's agent in its own app or in a third-party AI assistant that hosts MCP apps.

Shopify's generative discovery model (14 minute read)

Shopify deployed a shared generative discovery model for search and recommendation, leveraging semantic-ID tokens to enhance product personalization and relevance. The model improved online and offline metrics, such as a 9.85% lift in conversion rate and significant gains in search relevance.

OpenAI open-sources MCP Extensions for ChatGPT-native plugins (1 minute read)

The TypeScript and Python packages add ChatGPT-specific features to MCP servers and apps, including sidebar entry points, custom file viewers, composer resource search, and thumbnail part pickers. The SDKs ship with a Bits & Bolts demo plugin and a written spec.

Reed Albergotti

Nvidia without Huang is like Apple without Jobs: A cash spigot without real innovation

Carlos Fuentes/File Photo/Reuters

Some Silicon Valley executives are quietly celebrating Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia and the national furor over chip exports to China. The good news for American companies is that tech exports that were going to China are now expected to be redirected to US firms, one person told me. That could accelerate the growth of the big AI labs and other Silicon Valley companies, and hobble Chinese rivals.

In the short term, they’re probably right. There’s strong evidence that export controls have successfully slowed China’s technological progress. The problem is that the US can’t win the technological race with China in the long term by slowing its rival down. The bigger and more difficult part of that victory is speeding up American innovation.

And that’s where Huang’s ouster is a counter-force to the gains made on China policy. Huang is one of Silicon Valley’s great innovators. In the short term, his ouster won’t be terrible for Nvidia. Nvidia may actually become a more profitable company now, because any new CEO will optimize for profitability, as Apple did under Tim Cook. Innovators burn a lot of money thinking about the long term. And Nvidia will never be as innovative as it was under Huang.

Huang was Nvidia’s one-man, long-term moat. That’s especially true now, in an era when AI allows pretty much any company to design a chip just like Nvidia’s, as OpenAI did in a matter of months.

A less innovative Nvidia is not just a problem for Nvidia. It’s a problem for the entire technology ecosystem. Big, powerful incumbents tend to be barriers to innovation. Cook’s Apple built the iPhone and then sat on that invention by defending its turf — a great business strategy but one that let the entire mobile ecosystem stagnate.

The key risk to the US tech industry isn’t that Chinese spies will steal its cutting-edge technology. It’s that Silicon Valley is at risk of seeing the magic formula that brought that technology into being in the first place weakened.

Succession Crisis

by Andrew Egger

Last Wednesday, while most Republicans were still shaking off the shell shock of their historic midterms drubbing, Mike Pence was already launching his latest attempt at a party takeover.

“This midterm election wasn’t a rout, it was a reckoning,” Pence wrote in an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal. “The American people have rejected our party’s shift toward economic populism.” Trump’s first vice president ticked through a list of failures: The out-of-control deficit spending, the unconstitutional tariffs, the abandonment of anti-abortion policy, and the seizure of stakes in private companies. The war in Iran, which had become an “albatross” thanks to the administration’s willingness to pursue a diplomatic solution “rather than allowing our troops to finish off the threat posed by the Iranian regime, once and for all.”

“With the next presidential election on the horizon, we must decide what we’re for before we decide whom we’re for,” Pence concluded. “We can return the Republican Party to the timeless principles that have led to our greatest successes and, more important, have made America strong, prosperous, and free.”

Both Pence and the yesteryear conservative ideas he stands for have fallen far out of favor in the Trump-era GOP. The new MAGA hotness, ideologically speaking, has been the national-conservative New Right that has grown up in the last decade to embrace Trump’s love of wielding government power, his hardcore tariff protectionism, and his (supposed) antipathy for stupid foreign wars.

No better place to watch the factions fight! Join our pro-democracy community.

Join

For the New Right, Trump’s 2024 election represented their near-permanent vanquishing of the faction they deride as “zombie Reaganism.” The final cataclysm was supposed to come in 2028, with a seamless handoff of the GOP imprimatur from Trump to their truest ideological champion, JD Vance.¹ But the plan has gone awry: Trump is damaged goods, Vance’s future is in doubt, and the zombie Reaganites are starting to haul themselves back out of the graves. The natcons are grabbing their chainsaws to try to put the threat down early.

One new group that launched to that end just this week is American Ascent, a Vance-allied organization backed by $12 million from New Right megadonor Tom Klingenstein. American Ascent is positioning itself as a candidate-recruitment organization hoping to mold the next generation of national conservative Republican lawmakers. They cast their ideological project in generational terms: Last week’s midterms wipeout had been a “complete rebuke of the type of Republicans that were in Congress,” the organization’s vice president told Politico this week. “Old ideas are for old people.” Translation: We’re not going back.

This fight has been coming for a while. For the last decade, GOP politics have been organized so tightly around the personal cult of Donald Trump—as anti-ideological a politician as we have seen on the national scene in living memory—that fights over the policy direction of the future party have been pushed to the side. The wins the New Right has notched have been more positional than ideological: Trump has perceived them as the truer and more loyal allies to his person, and relied on them to staff his administration. But there are plenty of old-school conservative voters left in the GOP coalition. And even as the natcons have colonized professional D.C.—staging hostile takeovers at old Reaganite redoubts like the Heritage Foundation—the old-school professional class has maintained a beachhead at organizations like Pence’s Advancing American Freedom.

The intra-right fight has been accelerated by Trump’s sudden midterm implosion. All at once, the end of MAGA as America’s dominant political force is less of a future likelihood than an immediate present reality.

And the New Right has a new problem: After years of benefiting enormously from their closeness to Trump himself, they now find themselves partially paralyzed by that same proximity. The Penceheads can get right on with planning for a post-Trump future; the Vanceguard, like Vance himself, are stuck with the ongoing Trump present.

Groups like American Ascent are thus pulled awkwardly in two directions: They’re trying to cast themselves both as Trump’s inheritors and as the fearless defenders of his agenda against those who would try to dilute it—even on issues like immigration, where Trump himself is suddenly and unexpectedly moderating his tone. At the same time, they’re trying to portray themselves as the generational-change future of the party—even as they tie themselves unambiguously to the catastrophic recent past.

“[Trump] will be the leader of the party until he decides that he doesn’t want to be politically active anymore,” American Ascent spokesman Bradley Devlin told me on a press call this week. “That could mean that he’s the president, it could mean that he’s not president.” Republican candidates, Devlin said, should still expect to make a pilgrimage to Mar-a-Lago to seek Trump’s blessing if they want to get anywhere in 2028 and beyond.

All this presents an opportunity for other factions—although whether Pence is right that a sizable chunk of the party’s voters yearn for a return to his “timeless principles” remains to be seen. That’s the same case Pence made, after all, when he ran for president in 2024. He never topped 10 percent in the primary polls, and dropped out long before the Iowa caucuses. Still, it’s not like he was the only one: Plenty of other Republican notables, from Ron DeSantis to Marco Rubio, still share some of the old Reaganite DNA.

The GOP oldheads may never regain their old position of control in the party. But Pence is probably right about one thing: They’ll never have a better opportunity to press their case than the one they’ve got right now.

LUTNICK SWEATS: The knives are out for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who seems to be taking much of the blame internally for the White House’s remarkable exposure to the Jensen Huang Nvidia scandal. Axios reports that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick last week over his failure to add the company Megaspeed (an apparent front company for illicit Chinese chip imports led by Huang’s alleged Chinese-spy paramour) to a government list of companies flagged as national security threats:

The Commerce Department oversees the export of sensitive U.S. technologies and Lutnick’s actions—or lack thereof—are increasingly under scrutiny following revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with Megaspeed employee and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang.

At a White House Situation Room meeting on Thursday after the midterm elections, Bessent pressed Lutnick on why Megaspeed had not been added to the Commerce Department’s entity list, to which Lutnick responded he would “look into it.”

Poor Lutnick—just when you think you’ve made it through the Epstein scandal intact, here comes another horndog squillionaire to put you right back in the doghouse. Read the whole thing.

PROTEINMAXXING: It’s official: Mississippi has gone blue. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith conceded to Democratic challenger Scott Colom yesterday, bringing the official tally of Senate Democrats to 55 with Alaska still technically too close to call. Colom will be Mississippi’s first black senator in more than 140 years. Meanwhile, the burger-flipping dude from the viral Colom ad who said “Pick another protein? SO LONG, VIVEK: Vivek Ramaswamy appears to be stepping away from the spotlight for a while. Since getting clobbered by Amy Acton in the Ohio governor’s race last week, Ramaswamy hasn’t posted anything except his concession speech to his 3.5 million X followers. And yesterday, a new statement popped up in his X bio: “Account is not actively managed.”

It’s an ignominious end—or hiatus?—for the public life of the biotech billionaire turned MAGA politico, who tried to speedrun his way into GOP relevance by combining MAGA-didn’t-go-far-enough politics with madcap TED-talk founder energy. After spending a few years trying to establish himself as a right-wing thought leader—writing a blizzard of op-eds on COVID policy and a trilogy of unreadable anti-woke books—he elbowed his way into electoral politics by self-funding a 2024 presidential run before dropping out and endorsing Trump after the Iowa caucuses. (He was also briefly involved in DOGE before the other manic tech-bro mega-MAGA billionaire crowded him out.)

Vivek seemed to think running for governor in Ohio would be an easier hill to climb. But he couldn’t hit a baseball, failed to lift a child, and released one of the most self-destructive, morally bankrupt TV ads in modern political history. Now he finds himself one of the most unambiguous losers of the midterms. And he doesn’t even have the testicular fortitude to post through it.

Ben Tossell

Nov 12

READ IN APP

Now I’m having fun!

My Ramp post was really well received with one or two ‘I’m not sure what I just looked at’ comments (which is totally fair).

The best I can describe what I’m doing now is exploring people and companies who are having fun with AI, doing things differently, being authentic and succeeding.

Which is basically how I want to describe my ‘work’.

But I think a lot of people are living in fear. Scared they’re behind, they’re not doing enough, others using AI ‘better’ than them, where’s there job going etc.

I want to focus on using AI for fun.

AI is a tool, you need one agent app (I’ve been using Droid with Opus 5.5 medium, fast mode for my posts, fable here and there). Use the tool to do work beyond what you could do before, don’t think about how you can finally optimise every aspect of every little thing. (I’ve basically stopped using Grok Bot, except telling me when the tennis is on).

As part of my explorations I’m working on a new post for another company I admire and who do things very differently. Coming next week…

“Everyone judges a book by its cover”

Can you guess which company it is?

And yes, these animations are staying. Honestly I love them. I love making them too.

So much so that I set up a sophisticated camera set up to monitor what my days look like and here’s the footage.

Morning voice dump. Kids. Stickmen.

What to know about this year’s UN climate talks

Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists have gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual UN climate talks. But this year’s negotiations are taking place against a particularly tense geopolitical backdrop, as the world falls further behind the Paris Agreement’s goals.

Energy prices are soaring, and there are big questions about how countries will tackle the climate crisis. Expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance, and whether negotiators can agree on meaningful action.

One more thing

How Chinese short dramas became AI content machines

China’s short drama industry is fueled by bite-sized, melodramatic, and smutty shows built for smartphone scrolling. Now, many are being made entirely with AI: no actors, camera operators, cinematographers, or CGI specialists required.

An average of 470 AI-generated short dramas were released every day in January. Production timelines have shrunk from months to weeks, while costs have dropped by up to 90%. Storytelling is also increasingly driven by performance data.

The format is rapidly expanding overseas while reshaping the work of writers and production crews. Read the full story on AI’s dramatic impact on China’s short drama industry.

—Caiwei Chen

Ryanggang Province sits on the upper reaches of the Yalu River, which divides North Korea and China. Because the river is narrow there, the province historically saw more defections than anywhere else. Pochon County lies about one kilometer upstream from Hyesan, the provincial capital, and the river there is only 20 to 30 meters wide. Using the COVID-19 pandemic as a pretext, the Kim Jong-un regime reinforced the barbed-wire fencing along the Yalu River and installed large numbers of surveillance cameras, sealing the border under two or three layers of security. Crossing into China was thought to have become impossible.

Soaring prices strain North Korean winter preparations Daily NK

Coal prices in Sinuiju have climbed past 2 million North Korean won per metric ton this month, as a weakening currency is driving up the cost of nearly everything families need to survive the 2026 winter. Sinuiju is North Korea’s largest city on the Chinese border and the capital of North Pyongan province. Families there and across the province are busy making kimchi, stockpiling heating fuel and repairing their homes before the cold sets in. Soaring prices in the country’s private markets, known as jangmadang, have turned these yearly chores into a heavy financial burden. Many households now struggle to cover even the basics of winter preparation.

Lee set to attend Asean, APEC summits as North Korea diplomacy speculation intensifies JoongAng Daily

President Lee Jae Myung will take a four-day trip next week to attend Asean-related summits in Manila, the Philippines, and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China, the Blue House announced Thursday. Lee will depart Monday for a two-day visit to Manila to attend meetings with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and partner countries, then head to Shenzhen in China’s southern Guangdong Province Wednesday to take part in the APEC summit, National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac said in a press briefing at the Blue House in central Seoul.

Hyesan street food vendors squeezed by soaring prices Daily NK

Street food vendors in Hyesan are struggling to survive as ingredient costs soar in November 2026. Raising prices drives customers away, but holding prices steady leaves vendors with almost no profit. Hyesan sits on the Yalu River across from Changbai, China, in North Korea’s mountainous north. The city is the capital of Ryanggang province, and its markets depend heavily on cross-border trade. “Street food vendors in Hyesan are very frustrated,” a source in Ryanggang province told Daily NK on Friday. The vendors sell tofu rice, artificial meat rice, rice cakes and blood sausage to passersby on city streets.

So apparently United just told AI agents to stay out of its booking system. The airline restricted unauthorized third-party AI agents (the assistants that log in and click "buy" for you) from using its app and site, and from booking through travel agencies and aggregators. Here's the fight. If your assistant becomes the place your trip starts, the airline loses the customer relationship, much like it did to online travel sites. Amazon is playing the same game. Your AI agent might remember the headphones you returned because they hurt your ears, but apparently it still can't get past the gate agent.

😸 DeepMind's AlphaGenome 2 Predicts What a DNA Typo Does in Each Cell Type

Every cell in your body carries the same DNA, yet a single-letter change in it can cause disease in some cells and do nothing in others. Google DeepMind just released AlphaGenome 2, an AI model built to predict which cells a given DNA typo actually messes with.

To see why that's hard, you need one piece of setup. DNA holds genes, but it also holds regulatory switches, stretches that tell a cell how loudly to read a gene. Different cell types flip different switches. So a typo in one switch can leave a gut immune cell and a brain cell with very different volume settings on the same gene.

Earlier approaches mostly looked at whole tissues, which blurs everything together. It's like trying to figure out which fruit made your smoothie sour by tasting the whole smoothie. AlphaGenome 2 tastes each fruit. You hand it a 1-million-letter stretch of DNA plus one condition (a tissue, a cell type, or a cell state), and it predicts what that cell does with that DNA. Scientists can even build the condition from their own single-cell experiment. The model learned from more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues, from humans and mice.

Here's what DeepMind reports:

Nearly twice as many gene-changing variants found in cells as the previous best model.

On 28 immune cell types, 30% versus 16% for causal variants and 43% versus 23% for effect direction.

Reproduced a published gut-disease finding on a computer, tying a far-off switch to the ETS2 gene in gut macrophages (immune cells).

Adapted to new cell states from a few dozen cells with no retraining, and showed a severe-COVID variant hits activated T cells harder.

Those benchmark numbers come from DeepMind's own evaluation, and the model is for research only, not validated for clinical or diagnostic use. Still, the part I'd repeat to a friend is the shift in the question. Instead of asking whether a typo is bad, scientists can ask who it's bad for. That's a much more useful question for anyone studying a disease that only shows up in one organ.

It also guesses properties nobody measured from one measurement they did, which can help labs decide which experiments to run next. And DeepMind precomputed predictions for trait-linked variants across hundreds of conditions, covering traits from height to type 2 diabetes, so researchers don't have to run the model themselves for those.

Researchers can use it now for non-commercial work through the AlphaGenome API, with Colab tutorials, and there's a private preview for commercial research. DeepMind says it explains more of the differences between cell types even in DNA regions outside its training data. The test that matters next is whether outside labs get the same results on cells and regions the model never saw.

Why this matters: Drug development mostly fails, with only about 10% of drug programs that reach human trials winning approval. Targets backed by human genetics were found to be 2.6 times more likely to succeed, but a genetic hit rarely says which cell is involved. Predicting the effect cell type by cell type could help researchers pick the right target earlier, and it gives medicine a cleaner way to ask why one variant harms one organ and not another. That 2.6x figure covers genetic evidence in general, not this model, so think promising tool, not proven one.

Commercial medicine is a long way off. DeepMind says the model isn't validated for clinical or diagnostic use, so it won't read your genetic tests yet. Here's our estimate, not DeepMind's. Labs and drug companies use it over the next one to three years. A new medicine typically takes 10 to 15 years from discovery to approval, so a drug aimed at a target picked today lands between the mid-2030s and early 2040s. The thing to get excited about now is faster, better-aimed research, not a pill.

🎓 AI Skill of the Day: Check the Translation, Not Just the Answer

This week's Yang-Mills story (see Around the Horn below) holds a lesson you can use on your next spreadsheet. A computer can check a proof step by step using Lean, a proof-checking program that works a bit like spell-check for logic. But Lean only confirms that the proof matches the statement as written in Lean. Whether that statement matches the real math problem is a translation, and a human has to check it. That's why the committee's validation document spells out how it checked the Lean code against the standard problem statements. An earlier OpenAI proof reportedly had the same gap, with Lean verifying a weaker claim than the prose described. A perfectly spelled essay can still answer the wrong prompt.

Your version of this happens daily. Ask AI for revenue by customer and it may quietly use net revenue instead of gross, or active customers instead of all customers. The output looks flawless, and it answers a slightly different question than yours.

After the AI answers, ask it to list every definition and assumption it used, in plain English.

Compare that list to your original request word by word, and mark any term it narrowed, widened, or swapped.

Paste only your original request and that list into a fresh chat, so the first chat doesn't defend its own work, and ask it to hunt for mismatches.

Below is my original request and the definitions and assumptions an assistant used to answer it. List every place where a definition is narrower, broader, or different from my wording. For each one, tell me how the result would change if my original wording were used instead. MY REQUEST: [paste] THEIR DEFINITIONS AND ASSUMPTIONS: [paste]
